questions.stem: A 45-year-old HIV positive pajent develops a widespread rash after he was commenced on co-trimoxazole. You assess the rash and ciarry out a SCORTEN prognostic measurement. Which of the following is not a SCORTEN parameter in the assessment of toxic epidermal necrolysis?
questions.explanation:
SCORTEN has seven parameters which also include serum urea, tachycardia and skin detachment of >10% on the first day of assessment.
The higher the score, the higher the mortality risk (3-5% for one point and >90% for 6-7 points).
The SCORTEN should be measured every 3 days to assess the progress / deterioration.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old lady presented to the dermatologist with a 1-week history of painful tender subcutaneous nodules on the anterior aspects of both shins. Initially, tile "lumps" were very red and painful to touch and gradually the colour had changed to bruise-like. On examination, ankle swelling was noted. She denies other symptoms. What is the commonest cause of thiscondition in the U.K.?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is erythema nodosum, of which in the U.K. streptococcal throat infec tion is the commonest cause.
Other causes include sarcoidosis, yersinia, hellcobacter pylori infections, actinomycosis, tuberculosis, pregnancy and the combined contraceptive pill.
Measurement of anti-streptolysin titre 7-10 days following a sore throat can help confirm the streptococcal aetiology in retrospect.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old lady was recently treated with isoniazid for prophylaxis of tuberculosis. She presented with an erythematous butterfly rash on the cheeks following sun exposure and reports arthralgia and several mouth ulcers. Her full blood count showed normocytic anaemia, and slight reduced platelet count. Her renal function is normal. Which of the following auto-antibodies will most likely be positive?
questions.explanation:
Drug-induced lupus erythematosus, should be considered in older patients with no past history of connective tissue disorders. Anti-histone antibody is positive in the majority of patients with drug-induced lupus (>90%), positive ANA is also seen in these patients.
Common causes of drug-induced lupus include:
Allopurlnol
Clonidine
Danazol
Hydralazine
isoniazid
Lithium
Methyldopa
Penicillamine
In the majority of the cases, drug-induced lupus tends to spare the kidneys, however, if they are involved, double stranded DNA is often positive too.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy suffered from a sore throat for 2 weeks. Thereafter, he complained of abdominal pain, swollen ankles and a rash on the lower legs. Examination of the rash shows multiple areas of palpable petichiae and purpura. Skin biopsy showed evidence of small vessel vasculitis with IgA deposition in the vascular walls on direct immunofluoresence. What should be the next investigation performed?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is Henoch-Schonlein Purpura, which is usually a self-limiting small vessel vasculitis often seen in children and young adults following a sore throat.
Abdominal involvement can occur in around half of the patients.
Measurement of blood pressure and urinalysis to check for renal involvement is essential.
A small percentage of patients (less than 5%), may progress to chronic renal failure.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presented to Accident and Emergency for the third time in 1 month with a history of very painful right leg, fever (38°C), joint pains in fingers and knees and myalgia. His blood tests showed evidence of moderate renal impairment, and his father says that one of his cousins had a similar presentation and was treated successfully with colchicine. On examination there was a bright erythema of the leg, mimicking a cellulitis. He had marked raised C-Reactive Protein. The most likely diagnoses here is:
questions.explanation:
Familial Mediterranean fever is an autosomal recessive disorder due to pyrindefi ciency and presents with Intermittent fever, arthritis, cellulitis-like rash on the legs, myalgia and renal impairment.
Treatment with colchicine can be very effective, although more recently anti-IL 1 monoclonal antibody (anakinra) has been found to be very effective in all auto-inflammatory syndromes.
Hyper IgE syndrome presents with recurrent infections with raised serum IgE levels and skin changes which are similar to atopic dermatitis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a long history of recurrent sinusitis and ear infections. She pre.;ented a month ago to Accident and Emergency with haemoptysis which was thought to be secondary to a ch.,st infection. She was febrile (temperature 38.7°C) and has lost 1 stone in weight over 6 weeks. You note that she has a collapsed nasal bridge, resulting in a saddle nose appearance. Which of the following investigations is most likely to be positive?
questions.explanation:
Wegener's granulomatosis presents with recurrent sinusitis, ear involvement, and respiratory Involvement with haemoptysis, arthralgia and saddle nose shape due to collapsed nasal bridge.
Cutaneous involvement is found in around a third of patients, anci often consists of painful small ulcers or vasculitic palpable purpura.
c-ANCA is positive in around 80-90% of the patients.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of multiple crusted areas on his scalp, face and central chest. He gives a dear history of flaccid bullae that rupture easily leaving eroded areas that crust. There is no mucosal involvement. Treatment with anti-fungal creams for presumed seborrhoeic dermatitis failed to clear the lesions. Biopsy of one of the lesions showed acantholysis confined to the sub-corneal area and deposits of IgG in the epidermis on immunofluorescence. Which antigen is involved in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Pemphigus foliaceus is a milder variant of pemphigus vulgaris with flaccid bullae progressing to crusted erosions in a seborrhoeic distribution.
Mucosal involvement is typically absent, and the defect is high in the epidermis in the sub-corneal layer.
Oesmoglein-1 can also be found in pemphigus vulgaris and pemphigus vegetans.
However, in pemphigusvulgaris, Desmoglein 3 is almost always present as well.
Collagen VII is the target antigen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Laminin-6 is targeted in cicatricial pemphigoid.
BP-180 and BP-230 are the auto-antigens targeted in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man developed multiple yellow plaques on the peri-orbital skin. Some of the plaques were ulcerated with a few having a telangiectatic component. Biopsy from one of the lesions showed a palisading granuloma with necrobiosis and foamy histiocytes with giant Touton cells. The most appropriate next investigation in this patient would be:
questions.explanation:
Paraproteinaemia is found in nearly three quarters of the cases of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma.
This is predominantly IgG, however, IgM paraproteinaemia may also occur.
Cryoglobulinaemia can also occur in about a third of the patients; therefort:
cryoglobulin studies should also be performed.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old 34-weeks pregnant lady in her third pregnancy developed multiple urticated plaques on her thighs and abdomen with a large urticated plaque involving her umbilicus with some vesicles. She is otherwise well but is extremely concerned about her pregnancy. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is true?
options: A pregnancy termination is often required.
Biopsy and immunofluorescence findings would be non-specific in this condition.
There is a slightly increased risk of premature labor.
This condition has no effect on the foetus and always resolves following post-partum.
This condition tends to continue many years after delivery.
questions.explanation:
Pemphigoid gestationis is a rare pregnancy-related dermatosis that often occurs in the second or third trimester.
It typically presents with urticated plaques or vesicles and bullae, often with umbilical involvement.
There is an Increased risk for prematurity and small for gestational age babies, and less than 10% risk of the neonates have skin lesions.
The condition almost always resolves post-partum, and does not tend to progress to a chronic stage.
immunofluorescence typically shows linear C3 +/- IgG along the basement membrane zone and can be very helpful in distinguishing this condition from the urticated phase of pruritic papules and plaques of pregnancy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the commonest recognized cause of recurrent erythema multiforme?
questions.explanation:
Although many factors can trigger erythema multiforme, herpes simplex virus (HSV)
is the commonest known trigger for this self-limiting condition.
In the absence of any identifiable trigger, a long-term (6-24 months) suppressive therapy for HSV such as aciclovir 400 mg twice daily can be given for recurrent erythema multiforme.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man presents with keratotic beaded papules on the nape of the neck. Which of the following disorders is not associated with elastosis perforans serpiginosa?
questions.explanation:
Elastosis perforans serpiginosa is a perforating disorder characterized by transepidermal elimination of elastic fibers.
Hyperkeratotic papules varying from 2 mm to 1 cm in diameter occur in a serpiginous distribution.
0-penicillamine is associated with the development of elastosis perforans serpiginosa.
The neck is most commonly involved.
Elastosis perforans serpiginosa is associated with Down's syndrome, acrogeria, Marfan's syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, cutis laxa, osteogenesis imperfecta, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome and pseudoxanthoma elasticum.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about immunology of bullous pemphigoid is false?
options: Elevated serum IgE levels correlate with the presence of pruritus.
Peripheral blood eosinophilia correlates with serum IgE levels.
Peripheral blood eosinophilia is seen in 90% patients.
Serum IgE is elevated in 50% patients.
Serum IgE levels correlate with IgG anti-basement membrane zone immunofluorescence titers.
questions.explanation:
Almost 50% of patients with bullous pemphigoid have elevated total serum IgE.
Levels of serum IgE positively correlate with IgG anti-basement membrane zone immunofluorescence titers.
Elevated levels of IgE correlate with thepresence of pruritus.
90% of patients have peripheral blood eosinophilia.
Peripheral blood eosinophilia does not correlate with serum IgE levels.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not useful in differentiating epidermolysis bullosa acquisita from porphyria cutanea tarda?
options: Absence of hirsutism in sites affected by epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
IgG and complement deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Immune deposits around the dermal blood vessels in porphyria cutanea tarda.
Negative urine porphyrin screen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Sclerodermoid skin changes and photo distribution of rash in porphyria cutanea tarda.
questions.explanation:
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita may mimic bullous pemphigoid, porphyria cutanea tarda, pseudo-porphyria, bullous lupus erythematosus, cicatritial pemphigoid, linear IgA bullous dermatosis, Brunsting-Perry cicatricial bullous pemphigoid, dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa and rarely other disorders like toxic epidermal necrolysis and dermatitis herpetiformis.
Although the presentation of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita may be reminiscent of porphyria cutanea tarda, these patients do not have other hallmarks of porphyria cutanea tarda or pseudo-porphyria, such as hirsutism, a photodistributionof the eruption, or scleroderma-like changes.
Urinary porphyrlns are within normal limits in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Patients with porphyria cutanea tarda, which may mimic epidermolysis bullosa acquisita clinically, frequently have IgG and complement deposits at the dermo-epider mal junction similar to those of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita patients.
Porphyria cutanea tarda skin also demonstrates immune deposits around the dermal blood vessels, which distinguishes it from epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient is referred with yellow nails. He has a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following statements regarding yellow nail syndrome is incorrect?
options: Can be associated with internal malignancies.
Can be associated with lichen planus.
High doses of vitamin E may be helpful.
Patients report failure of nail growth.
questions.explanation:
Yellow nail syndrome may or may not be associated with a systemic disorder.
It is a triad of yellow nails, primary lymphoedema, and pleural effusion.
Nail features include thickening, transverse ridging, diminished growth, increased curvature with a "hump," and onycholysis.
It is occasionally familial.
Respiratory tract involvement is seen and features include sinusitis, bronchiectasis, pleural effusions, upper respiratory infections and pneumonia.
Other conditions that may be associated with yellow nail syndrome include rheumatoid arthritis and internal malignancies.
Patients always claim that their nails have stopped growing.
High oral doses of vitamin E may be beneficial.
Spontaneous improvement is possible.
Topical vitamin E and systemic antifungal medications (itraconazole, fluconazole) do not appear to be effective.

questions.stem: Proximal nail splinter haemorrhages are seen in all the following except:
questions.explanation: The following are causes of proximal nail splinter haemorrhages: bacterial endocarditis, trichinosis, anti-phospholipid syndrome and altitude sickness.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions can give a keratoderma-like yellow appearance of the palms?
questions.explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis and pregnancy can give palmar erythema.
Limited systemic sclerosis (CREST) gives telangiectasia which can be found on the palms.
Hypothyroidism should always be included in the differential of "yellow palms" particularly when carotinaemia is suspected.

questions.stem: The differential diagnosis of "punctate keratoderma" affecting the palms will include all except:
questions.explanation:
Punctate palmar keratoderma is an autosomal dominant keratoderma characterized by keratotic plugs, often limited to the palmar creases.
Cowden's syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition due to PTEN gene defect and can present with palmar keratoses, tricholemmomas, buccal cobblestoning, lipomas, thyroid gland lesions, high-arched palate and adenoid facies.
Follicular or syringotropic mycosis fungoides can present with palmar involvement but not with punctate keratoses.
Although palmar pits are often seen in Darier's disease, this condition can be associ ated with palmo-plantar keratoses too.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old lady with type-1diabetes develops waxy plaques on her shins. You diagnose these as Necrobiosis lipoidica. Which of the following statements regarding necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) is correct?
options: 30% of patients with diabetes will develop NL.
Less than 1% of diabetes patients will develop NL.
NL most frequently occurs on the upper trunk.
questions.explanation:
NL most commonly occurs on the shins and around two-thirds of its sufferers have diabetes.
Less than 1% of patients with diabetes develop NL.
The condition is difficult to treat and may develop areas of ulcerations.
Disease activity appears to be independent from glycaemlc control in diabetics.

questions.stem: You diagnose a patient with pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Which of the following is not a clinical variant/subtype of PG?
questions.explanation:
Another variant of PG includes the peri-stomal type which can particularly occur when the underlying inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is active.
PG can occur in IBD, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple myeloma and carcinoid tumour (rarely).
PG belongs to the group of neutrophilic dermatoses and may respond to corticosteroids, ciclosporin and anti-TNF therapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following subtypes of porokeratosis has the highest risk of malignant transformation?
questions.explanation:
Porokeratoses are a group of keratinizing disorders characterized histologically by the presence of a cornoid lamella which is a thin column of parakeratotic cells extending through the stratum corneum with absent granular layer and-occasionally-basal layer dyskeratosis.
The overall risk of transformation to squamous cell carcinoma is low but is highest with the linear subtype.
The commonest variant is disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis.
Giant porokeatosis of Mibelli can also be associated with a higher risk of malignancy transformation.

questions.stem: Milia can occur in some genodermatoses and are referred to as "primary milia". Secondary milia can occur in several disorders. In which of the following can milia occur as part of the disease process?
questions.explanation:
Milia are benign keratinous cysts.
Secondary causes of milia include subepidermal bullous formation (porphyria cutanea tarda, bullous pemphigoid, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita), radiotherapy, thermal burns, acne and allergic contact dermatitis.
Porphyria cutanea tarda presents clinically with skin fragility, bullae, erosions, milia and hypertrichosis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with end-stage renal failure who attends the haemodialysis unit developed an indurated tender subctaneous plaque on the inner aspect of her right thigh. A reticulate pattern of erythema was evident on her thigh. Biopsy from the lesion which included the subcutaneous fat showed calcification of small vessels with necrosis. In addition to haemodialysis, which other risk factor contributes to the development of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Calciphylaxis(also called "calcific uraemic arteriopathy") is a disease with a high mortality rate and occurs in the setting of renal failure, particularly in dialysis-dependent patients.
Risk factors include obesity, warfarin use, diabetes mellitus, liver disease, systemic steroid use, raised serum calcium and phosphate product, and raised serum aluminium.
Warfarin may alter the balance of calcification promoters and inhibitors and may need to be switched to heparin.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the gold standard in the diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita?
questions.explanation:
Although all the listed options are helpful in establishing the diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita by differentiating it from other immunobullous disorders like bullous pemphigoid, immuno-electron microscopy still remains the gold standard in the diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita lesions have Immune deposits within the sub-lamina densa zone of basement membrane zone.
Deposits in bullous pemphigoid are higher up in the hemidesmosome area or the lamina lucida area of the basement membrane.
In cicatricial pemphigoid, antigenic targets are confined to the lamina lucida.
Western blots of human skin basement membrane proteinscontain type VII collagen.
A new ELISA developed from recombinant, purified, post-translationally modified NC-1In stably transfected human cells is considered more sensitive than immunofluorescence and Western blotting and very specific for antibodies to type VII collagen.

questions.stem: Which one of the following forms of pemphigus involves non-stratified squamous epithelium?
questions.explanation: Paraneoplastic pemphigus is the only form of pemphigus that has involvement of non-stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not seen at an increased incidence in dermatitis herpetiformis?
questions.explanation:
Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with an increased risk for the following:
Gastrointestinal diseases, including: achlorhydria, atrophic gastritis, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease, malabsorption and bone loss.
Malignancies, including: gastrointestinal and non-Hodgkin's lymphomas.
Auto-immune diseases, including: thyroid disease, insulin-dependent diabetes, lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's syndrome, and vitiligo.
Neurologic diseases, including: epilepsy, ataxia, and dementia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the least common subtype of morphoea?
Auto-antibodies can be seen in morphea. Which of the following is not associated with auto-antibody positivity in morphoea?
questions.explanation:
Serum auto-antibodies have been found with variable frequency in patients with localized scleroderma.
Anti-nuclear antibodies usually with a homogenousimmunofluorescence pattern are most commonly found.
Anti-single stranded DNA and/or anti-histone antibodies may be found with extensive involvement.
Compared with other subsets of localized scleroderma, patients with generalized morphea have a higher frequency of antibody positivity which correlates with a more severe clinical presentation, greater number of lesions, more sclerotic lesions and longer duration of clinical course.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a recognized risk factor for development of Dupuytren's contracture?
questions.explanation:
Dupuytren's contracture (palmar fibromatosis) is a fibroproliferative disease.
Bilateral, progressive fibrosis of the palmar fascia.
Presenting most commonly as nodules over the fourth and fifth metacarpal head.
Joint contractures and flexion deformities may follow.
Significant risk factors for development of Dupuytren's contracture include old age, male sex (three to four fold increase), white northern European ancestry, family history, seizures, alcohol-induced liver disease, trauma, smoking, and diabetes mellitus.

questions.stem: All of these can be presenting features of Bazex syndrome exc€pt which one?
questions.explanation:
Bazex syndrome is an X-linked dominant syndrome, which is characterized by follicular atrophoderma, multiple basal cell carcinomas, hypotrichosis, and localized hypohidrosis.
The follicular atrophoderma presents as multiple ice-pick marks or patulous follicles (most commonly on the dorsal sides of the hands).
Associated findings may include facial hyperpigmentation,milia, hair shaft dystrophy, and multiple genital trichoepitheliomas.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with elastosis perforans serpiginosa?
questions.explanation:
Elastosis perforans serpiginosa is a perforating disorder characterized by transepider mal elimination of elastic fibers.
Hyperkeratoticpapules varying from 2 mm to 1 cm in diameter occur in a serpiginous distribution.
D-penicillamine is associated with the development of elastosis perforans serpiginosa.
The neck is most commonly involved.

questions.stem: Which of the following disorders gives an erythema contusiforme appearance?
questions.explanation: The tender erythematous warm nodules and raised plaques of erythema nodosum evolve into red or purplish colour to a yellow or greenish discoloration, resembling a deep bruise-erythema contusiforme.

questions.stem: Which of the following panniculitides can demonstrate an isomorphic phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Lupus panniculitis is a chronic recurrent panniculitis.
It is a mild variant of lupus erythematosus.
It is more frequent in women than men.
May present as subcutaneous nodules as the only clinical manifestation of the dis ease.
Histological features of discoid lupus erythematosus at the dermal-epidermal junction may be seen in only 20-30% patients.
Lobular panniculitis without vasculitis is the predominant histopathological feature.
An isomorphic phenomenon (Koebner) is frequently seen in patients with lupus panniculitis.
Subcutaneous erythematous nodules often develop or recur at the sites of trauma.
Treatments include topical, intralesional or oral corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine and dapsone.
An isomorphic phenomenon is also frequent In al-antitr ypsin-deficiencyassociated panniculitis.

questions.stem: Elevated levels of which of the following enzymes is predominantly implicated in pancreatic panniculitis?
questions.explanation:
Pancreatic panniculitis is also termed enzymatic fat necrosis.
It is associated with several pancreatic diseases, including acute and chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic carcinoma, pancreatic pseudocysts, vasculo-pancreatic fistulae, and drug induced pancreatitis.
In some patients there may be no demonstrable pancreatic disease.
Pancreatic enzymes, mostly lipase, seem to be responsible for the subcutaneous fat necrosis.
Presents as erythematous subcutaneous nodules around the ankles and knees that often ulcerate spontaneously.
Histopathologically, mostly lobular panniculitis without vasculitis is evident with an intense necrosis of the adipocytes at the centre of the fat lobules.
Ghost adipocytes are necrotic adipocytes, which have lost their nuclei and contain finely granular and basophilic material within their cytoplasm.
Ghost cells result from saponlfication-hydrolytic action of pancreatic enzymes on fat, followed by calcium deposition.
These ghost adipocytes are characteristic of pancreatic panniculitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following phenotypes is most commonly associated with cx1-antitrypsin-deficiency panniculitis?
questions.explanation:
The four major categories of a1-antitrypsin genes include: F (fast), M (medium), S (slow), and Z (very slow).
Two alleles determine the specific al-antitrypsin phenotype.
The most common allele associated with normal levels of a1-antitrypsin is M.
S and Z alleles are associated with low serum levels of the enzyme.
ZZ phenotype has severe al-antitrypsin deficiency.
Serious clinical manifestations include emphysema, hepatitis, cirrhosis, vasculitis, and angioedema.
Clinical manifestations of panniculitis include subcutaneous nodules on the lower abdomen, buttocks, and proximal extremities.
Other features include frequent ulceration and isomorphic phenomenon.
Histopathological features include lobular panniculitis without vasculitis, necrosis of the fat lobules with a dense inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils.
Dapsone is the mainstay treatment for mild disease.
For severe forms of the disease: intravenous infusion of exogenous al-proteinase inhibitor concentrate or genetically engineered al-antitrypsin can be used.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the commonest auto-immune disorder associated with vitiligo?
questions.explanation:
Vitiligo is frequently associated with auto-immune disorders.
The commonest is thyroid dysfunction, either hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) or hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's thyroiditis).
Other auto-immune disorders associated with vitiligo include Addison's disease, pernicious anemia, alopecia areata, and diabetes mellitus.
Patients with auto-immune polyendocrinopathy candidiasis ectodermal dystrophy also have an increased prevalence of vitiligo.

questions.stem: Which of the followingtreatments is recommended as first-line in the treatment of vulval lichen sclerosus (LS) according to the British Association of Dermatologists guidelines:
questions.explanation:
Clobetaol proprionate ointment is recommended as first-line treatment in vulval LS.
Although. all the other treatments can be used in this condition, very potent topical corticosteroids should be used first-line.
Suspect a concomitant allergic contact dermatitis to perfumes, topical anaesthetics and ciorticosteroids in resistant or "eczematized" cases, in particular with chronic syrnpto'11s and prolonged use of multiple topical agents.

questions.stem: A geographic tongue can be found in all the following conditio;,s except:
questions.explanation:
Down's syndrome is associated with macroglossia.
No specific treatment is required for geographic tongue.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false?
options: Buccal macules in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome may disappear over time.
Buccal mucosal macules are a pathognomonic feature of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
Mutation in the serine/threonine kinase 11 (STKll or LKBl) gene is responsible for more than half of all cases of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
Pigmented macules in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are absent at birth.
Tile most common malignancies associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are gastrointestinal.
questions.explanation:
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant malignant predisposition syndrome.
Mucocutaneous pigmentation and intestinal hamartomatous polyposis an:? hallmarks of the disease.
Small hyperpigmented macules appear on the lips and buccal mucosa in childhooo.
Pigmented lesions are not present at birth.
Up macules may disappear over time.
Macules of the buccal mucosa are pathognomonic and do not tend to disappear with time.
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is associated with internal malignancies.
Of the associated Internal malignancies, gastrointestinal (small intestine, colorectal, stomach, pancreas) malignancies are most common.
Surveillance is therefore required from an early age.
Mutation in the serine/threonine kinase 11 (STKll or LKBl) gene is responsible for more than half of all cases of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Granulomatous cheilitis represents acute onset of asymmtric swelling of the upper and less commonly lower lip.
Erythema, scaling, fissuring, and erosions may also develop.
There is prolonged and recurrent course with eventual fixed swelling.
Me.lkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is characterized by lingua plicata ("fissured" or fur rowed tongue), facial paralysis/ptosis, and granulomatous cheilitis.
Granulomatous cheilitis may be the sole manifestation of this syndrome.
Treatment of granulomatous cheilitis is generally unsatisfactory.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not associated with geographic tongue?
questions.explanation:
Geographic tongue is a benign inflammatory condition that affects 2% of the population.
It results from loss of filiform papillae.
Erythematous plaques are seen with an annular or serpiginous well-demarcated white border.
A changing geographic appearance is noted with time.
Incidence is increased in patients with more severe or early-onset psoriasis.
Treatment is not needed except in symptomatic patients in whom topical corticosteroids and analgesics may be useful.
Besides psoriasis, geographic tongue is seen in Reiter's syndrome and is associated with atopic dermatitis, diabetes mellitus, anaemia, hormonal disturbances, Down's syndrome, and lithium therapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with fissured tongue?
questions.explanation:
Fissured tongue (small irregular fissures on lateral dorsal tongue) is also known as lingua plicata and may be a normal variant.
It is also a classic but non-specific feature of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome.
Other associated conditions include psoriasis, Down's syndrome, acromegaly, and Sjogren syndrome.
Regular brushing of the tongue is emphasized to eliminate any associated bacterial overgrowth.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the aetiologic agent of oral hairy leukoplakia?
questions.explanation:
Oral hairy leukoplakia is an asymptomatic condition caused by Epstein-Barr virus.
It presents as corrugated, white plaques with accentuation ofthe vertical folds along the lateral borders of the tongue.
It occurs predominantly in immunosuppressed patients, especially HIV-infected individuals in which it is an AIDS-defining illness.
It may also occur in organ transplant recipients and in patients on chemotherapy.
It responds to aciclovir and cidofovir.
Other anecdotal treatments include topical retinoids, and podophyllin.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a known cause of macroglossia?
questions.explanation:
Disproportionate enlargement of the tongue relative to the jaw size is called macroglossia.
It may be congenital or acquired.
Pressure against the teeth results in scalloping along the lateral aspects of the tongue.
Problems Include difficulty with mastication and speech and accidental tongue biting are common.
Causes include Down's syndrome, hypothyroidism, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, neurofibromatosis, Infection by mycobacteria, filamentous bacteria, or fungus.
Macroglossia caused by amyloid deposition results in woody induration of the tongue.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not associated with periodontal disease?
questions.explanation:
Periodontal disease is associated with Human Immunodeficiency Virus, diabetel;, Down's syndrome, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
.... Additionally, children with Papillon-Lefevre syndrome also develop severe and destructive periodontal disease.
Treatment options include oral retinoids in Papillon-Lefevre syndrome, and external beam radiation in periodontal disease of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a recognized cause of gingival hyperplasia?
questions.explanation:
Causes of glngival hypertrophy include:
-Leuka,;,mi:: hyperplasia e.g. acute myeloblastic and myelomonocytic leukaemia.
-Glycogen storage disease type lb.
Medications e.g. phenytoin, calcium channel blockers, and ciclosporin.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true of cyclic neutropaenia?
options: Antibiotics do not help alveolar bone loss.
Oral ulcers recur at intervals of 21-27 days.
Ulcerative gingivostomatitis is the presenting feature.
questions.explanation:
Cyclic neutropaenia is an autosomal dominant disorder.
Acyclic decrease in the circulating neutrophils is seen.
It presents with ulcerative gingivostomatitis.
Oral lesions last few days and recur at 21 to 27 day intervals.
Progression to periodontal disease may be seen.
Alveolar bone loss may occur over time.
Spontaneous improvement is seen as neutrophil counts improve.
Systemic antibiotic therapy may prevent bone loss.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not associated with labial melanotic ma.:ules?
questions.explanation: Multiple lahial melanotic macules are associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Carney complex, and Laugier-Hunziker syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not associated with oral pigmentation?
questions.explanation:
Some medications may induce pigmentary changes of the oral mucosa.
Women appear more susceptible.
The common medications causing intra-oral pigmentary changes include minocycline, anti-malarials, clofazimine, amiodarone and zidovudine.
This acquired pigmentation fades after discontinuation of the implicated medication or it may persist for months to years.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man was admitted with a 6-week history of diarrhoea and burning micturition. He also complained of red, itchy eyes and lower back pain. Examination showed erosions on the glans penis. Which organism is most commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Reiter's syndrome comprises of classic triad of arthritis, non-gonococcal urethritis, and conjunctivitis.
It is also known as reactive arthritis and may be triggered following an enteric or urogenital infection.
Symptoms appear 1-3 weeks from onset of urethritis/cervicitis or diarrhoea.
It is associated with Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA)-827.
Dermatological features incude shallow painless ulcers on the meatus and glans penis in a circinate pattern-circinate balanitis.
Hyperkeratotic psoriasiform thickening of palmar/plantar skin may be seen-keratoderma blennorrhagica.
Onychodystrophy and superficial oral ulcers may be present.
The most commonly implicated enteric pathogen in reactive arthritis is Campylobacter.
Chlamydia is the most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis.

questions.stem: The commonest site for intra-oral squamous cell carcinoma is?
questions.explanation:
Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest type of oral carcinoma and 1s most commonly found in the floor of the mouth.
Squamous cell carcinoma is more common amongst smokers and can arise from a pre-existing plaque of leukoplakia, particularly the verrucous form.
Squamous cell carcinoma can arise on the lips, particularly in smokers and patients with actinic damage.

questions.stem: Cobblestoning of the gingiva can occur with all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is associated with intestinal polyps and typically presents with (peri)-oral lentigines.
Other oral manifestations of Crohn's disease include aphthous ulcerations and granulomatous cheilitis.
The cobblestoning in Darrer's disease is mostly apparent in the hard palate.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with known chronic plaque psoriasis and metabolic syndrome is suspected to have vulval psoriasis. Which of the following anatomical structures will most likely be involved?
questions.explanation:
Genital psoriasis typically presents in the context of more generalised psoriasis but can present in isolation.
Diagnostically helpful features include a symmetrical distribution, marked erythema, occasional fissuring and healing without scarring.
First-line treatment is with a weak or moderate potency steroid.
Bland emollients play an important role in protecting against chemical and mechanical irritation and subsequent koebnerization.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old patient has an extremely itchy glistening orange-red plaque over the glans penis and foreskin. You suspect a diagnosis of plasma cell (or Zoon's) balanitis. What is the most definitive treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The cause of plasma cell balanitis/vulvitis is not known but established risk factors include poor hygiene and being uncircumcised
Whilst all the listed treatments listed can be used for plasma cell balanitis, only circumcision is reliably curative

questions.stem: What is the risk of developing complicating squamous cell carcinoma in patients with vulval lichen sclerosus?
questions.explanation:
Lichen sderosus is associated with an increased risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma, necessitating long-term follow up.
By contrast, penile disease is extremely unlikely to progress to squamous cell carcinoma with only one case reported In the literature.
Extra-genital disease, typically involving asymptomatic white patches with the appearance of cigarette paper, occurs in around 10 % of cases. There is no associated risk of squamous cell carcinoma at these sites.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the cardinal feature of Miescher-Melkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome?
questions.explanation:
.. Both Miescher-fJlelkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome and Melkersson-Rosenthal Syn drome are part of the orofacial granulomatosis disease spectrum, which can demonstrate all the listed features
Miescher-Melkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome is characterised by granulomatous change confined to the lips
Melkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome is characterised by granulomatous change involving the lips, tongue together with facial nerve paralysis.. Strictly speaking, orofacial granulomatosis is a diagnosis of exclusion that can only be made once systemic granulomatous disease such as Crohn disease, sarcoidosis, TB, Wegener's granulomatosis and allergic contact dermatitis have been expiored and excluded
Food allergies have been proposed to play a role and in some cases a benzoate/cinnamon-free diet can lead to improvement

questions.stem: Which of the following causes of genital ulceration is not a venereal disease?
questions.explanation:
Recurrent genital ulcerations is a minor criterion for the diagnosis of Beh et's dis ease.
Other non-venereal causes of genital ulcerations include trauma, tumours, tuberculosis, aphthosis, vesiculobullousdisoroers, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and chemical irritants.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl has developed very painful erosions in the vulva one week following unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner. Close examination showed a few intact vesicles on an erythematous base and few eroded areas where previous vesicles were present. The most likely pathogen in this case is:
questions.explanation:
Although traditional teaching is that herpes simplex virus type 1 is predominantly implicated in orolabial herpes and herpes simplex type 2 in genital herpes, both conditions can be caused by either viral serotypes.
Varicella-zoster virus is implicated in shingles, and whilst there are some reports of painful ulceration with fever in females with Epstein Barr Virus.
The morphology of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base is characteristic of herpes simplex Infection.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with peri-anal ulceration. The differential diagnosis of such ulceration includes:
questions.explanation:
A detailed history and skin examination is required to assess or obtain any valuable clues to the possible aetiology of chronic peri-anal ulceration.
Viral infections such as cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus should be suspected in immunocompromised patients.
Squamous cell carcinoma should be included in the differential-particularly if human papillomavirus infection isa risk.
Active underlying Crohn's disease can lead to metastatic disease which can present with ulceration. The histology in this case will show granulomas.
Genital involvement in Crohn's is often accompanied by oedema.
Nicorandil use has been incre.:isingly recognized to cause mucosal and cutaneous ulcerations, including in·peri-stomal sites.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old lady was recently discharged from the cardiology ward following a second myocardial infarction. She presents with a 6-week history of painful ulcer in the buccal mucosa. The ulcer was oval shaped with an erythematous halo and was extremely tender to touch. She reports no othe;mucosal ulceration and remains well otherwise. She is on a number of cardiac medications. Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of her oral ulceration?
questions.explanation:
Nicorandil has been increasingly linked to ulceration, both mucosal as well as cuta neous.
Recently, several reports have reported peri-stomal ulcerations and spontaneous bowel perforations.
These only respond to withdrawal of the nicorandil, however healing can take several months.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old patient has erosive lichenoid lesions in the oral mucosa. Which of the following is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
There are reports of association between lichen planus and hepatitis C virus infec tion, chronic active hepatitis, and primary biliary cirrhosis.
Hepatitis should be considered in patients with widespread or unusual presentations of lichen planus.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with 20-year history of pigmentation on the lips. Further examination shows linear pigmentation of his fingernails. There is no family history of similar features and his general health has been fine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Laugier- Hunziker syndrome refers to the presence of orolabial pigmented macules and longitudinal melanonychia. It differs from Peutz-Jeghers syndrome in its sporadic occurrence and absence of gastrointestinal involvement.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of mouth ulcers and painful blistering eruption on the trunk accompanied by painful warty growths over the groin and axillae. Widespread erythematous and annular plaques with flaccid blisters on his trunk and limbs were present along with exophytic plaques on the axillae, groins and peri-anal skin. Extensive erosions were present on the buccal mucosa and papillomatous vegetating lesions on the angles of the mouth. Skin biopsy showed intra-epidermal neutrophilic microabscesses. Direct immunofluorescence and indirect immunofluoresence on rat bladder epithelium were negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Pyodermatitis-pyostomatitis vegetans is a rare disorder characterized by typical mucocutaneous lesions and histopathological changes of pemphigus vulgaris but negative immunofluorescence findings.
Clinical and histological differentiationofpyodermatitis-pyostomatitisvegetans from pemphigus vegetans can be impossible.
Oral involvement is seen in all cases and cutaneous Involvement in around 60% of patients with PD-PSV.
The occurrence of pustules on the gingiva is very suggestive of pyostomatitis vegetans.
Most patients with PD-PSV have underlying ulcerative colitis (around 50%) or Crohn's disease (around 10%).
A prompt response to corticosteroids helps differentiating PD-PSV from PY.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is seen with recurrent oral ulcerations. You suspect Behc;et's disease. The diagnosis of Behc;et's disease requires the presence of the major criterion and 2 of the minor criteria according to the International Study Group of Behc;et's Disease. Which of the following is the major criterion?
options: A non-follicular (predominantly acral) papulo-pustular acneiform eruption.
Recurrent genital ulcerations (3 or more) in 12 months.
Recurrent oral ulcerations (3 or more) per 12 months.
questions.explanation:
Beh et's disease is a neutrophilic dermatosis with a vasculitis which is more prevalent in the Middle East and Japan.
The minor criteria (of which at least 2 are required for the diagnosis) are recurrent genital ulcerations, uveitis or retinal vasculitis, cutaneous involvement (non-follicular papulo-pustular eruption or erythema nodosum) and a positive pathergy test.
Joint involvement with arthritis can occur but is not a minor criterion for the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a recognized risk factor for Peyronie's disease?
questions.explanation:
Peyronie's disease is fibrosis of the fibrous septa between the corpus spongiosum and the corpora cavernosa along the dorsum of the penis.
It is often associated with Dupuytren's contracture.
Risk factors include genetic predisposition, trauma to the penis, systemic vascular diseases, smoking and alcohol consumption.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presented with generalized tender macular erythema wh;ch was most prominent on the skin around his mouth and nose, and in the groin a,ea. Two days after his hospitalization, the erythematous rash started to desquamate, particularly in his groin area. He was feverish and appeared lethargic, but had no mucoul. membrane involvement and no lymphadenopathy. His mother said that he had a sore throat two days prior to his eruption and has not been on any medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is characterized by generalized tender macular erythema which desquamates within few days, particularly on the skin around the mouth, nose and flexural areas.
Typically, large superficial flaccid bullae may appear on the background of the erythema and leave painful denuded areas.
The child is often lethargic and febrile and the condition is due to staphylococcal exfoliating toxin.
Prompt treatment with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics results in fullrecovery and the prognosis is generally very good.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis would certainly be in the differential, however, this condition is often secondary to drugs and occurs more in adults than children, and often involves the mucous membranes.
Diagnostic biopsy is sometimes required to differentiate the two conditions.
In toxic epidermal necrolysis, full epidermal necrosis is seen with minimal dermal infiltrate.
The defect (split) in staphylococcalscalded skin syndrome is in the subcorneal layer.
Kawasaki's disease may give rise to desquamation in the flexural area; however, the diagnosis requires the presence of high fever lasting for at least five days and four of the following criteria: conjunctival injection, mucous membrane changes (particularly strawberry tongue appearance), erythema or oedema of the palms and soles, and cervical lymphadenopathy.
Coronary artery aneurysm is one of the main and fatal complications of Kawasaki's disease, and patients therefore require an echocardiogram.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man presented with a 10-year history of red-brown patches in the axillae with distinct borders and absence of any scaling. The condition was mildly pruritic and scrapings were negative for fungal hypahe or spores. Examination unde, Wood's light showed coral-pink fluorescence. The organism responsible for this condition is:
questions.explanation:
Erythrasma can be treated with topical or oral erythromycin.
Epidermophytonfloccosum may affect the axillae, although it is commonly present in the groins.
It is a fungus that does not fluoresce; scrapings can be positive for microscopy and culture.
Trichophyton verrucosum is a zoophilic dermatophyte found in cattle and usually results in a severe inflammatory dermatomycosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms causes cutaneous larva migrans?
questions.explanation:
Cutaneous larva migrans is a pruritic eruption that is caused by the nematode hook worm Ankylostoma brazilense (and in some occasions Ankylostoma caninum), which is deposited in dogs and cats faeces.
It clinically presents with serpiginous vesicular burrows that migrate slowly. The worm cannot penetrate the basement membrane.
Stronglyoides stercoralis, another nematode, causes cutaneous larva c1.irrens which presents similarly with serpiginous urticarial burrows on the buttocks or trunk. This worm however can penetrate the basement membrane and can affect the lungs and the gastrointestinal tract. When it does involve the lungs it may cause Loeffler's syn drome (pulmonary eosinophilia).
Schistosomes may cause schistosomiasis and "swimmer's" itch.
Mycobacterium marinum causes fish tank granuloma presenting with red to purple coloured nodules and plaques with sporotrichoid spread.
A further difference between Stronglyoides and Ankylostoma is that the latter mi grates slowly and Stronglyoides typically migrate fast.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for (recurrent) cellulitis?
questions.explanation:
Although alcohol and smoking are thought to increase the possible risk for cellulitis, this has not been proven in any study.
Lymphoedema is the strongest risk factor for the development of cellulitis followed by leg ulcers.
The risk of cellulitis increases after each episode due to post-cellulitis residual oedema (mostly secondary lymphoedema) and all the above mentioned factors need to be taken into account when managing patients with cellulitis.

questions.stem: In which group of patients will staphylococcalscalded skin syndrome be associated with a poor prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Conditions associated with poor prognosis in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) include diabetes and haemodialysis.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is the main differential diagnosis; however TEN involves the entire epidermis as opposed to SSSS in which the split is at the granular layer.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of slightly pruritic scaly hypopigmented patches on the shoulders and back which worsen following sun exposure. Examination showed hypopigmented patches with some fine scaling and no loss of hair colour within the patches. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Pityriasisversicolor is caused by the yeast Pityrosporumorbiculare, a lipophilic yeast hence it thrives on the sebaceous-rich areas of the back.
Increased temperature and humidity leads to worsening of the condition.
Vitiligo presents with depigmented patches with no epidermal change.
Poliosis (loss of hair colour) is a sign in vitiligo.
Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis is an idiopathic condition in which porcelain-white small macules appear predominantly on the lower legs.
Hypopigmented patches can represent rare variants of sarcoidosis and mycosis fungoides.

questions.stem: The "two-feet one hand syndrome" refers to the involvement of both feet and a single hand in:
questions.explanation:
This phrase is used to describe the occurence of tinea manum (often the dominant hand) associated with bilateral tinea pedis.
The commonest cause of tinea pedis is Trichophyton rubrum followed by Trichophyton interdigitale.
Psoriasis, atopic, allergic contact dermatitis as well as mycosis fungoides can all affect both the hands and feet.

questions.stem: Which of the following human papillomavirus serotype is not associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis?
questions.explanation:
Epidermodysplasia verruciformis present clinically as plain pink to skin-coloured flat papules similar to plain warts.
Epidermodysplasia verruciformis is associated with serotypes 3, 5, 8 and 12.
HPV-16 and 18 are associated with Bowen's disease, Bowenoid papulosis and cervical cancer.
Histologically, epidermodysplasia verruciformis is characterised by pale keratinocytes in the upper part of the epidermis.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man who is seriously ill in intensive care with neutropaenia on a background of chronic myeloid leukaemia developed several erythematous and purpuric macules on his thigh and lower back, which rapidly developed into haemorrhagic bullae which ruptured leaving ulcers with eschars. There was a surrounding erythematous violaceous necrotic area of skin. Blood cultures will most likely show which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Ecthyma gangrenosum is often a manifestation of sepsis secondary to pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Predisposing causes include neutropaenia, haematological malignancies, immunodeficiency syndromes, chemotherapy, burns and indwelling catheters.
The main differential diagnosis is of pyoderma gangrenosum which is not associated with septicaemia.
In rare cases, ecthyma gangrenosum can be caused by other organisms such as escherichia coli and neisseria meningitidis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old Caucasian man, who works for an international company recently returned from a foreign trip where he was working for six months. He recalled being bitten by an insect on his right cheek arid gradually developed a small papule which has become ulcerated. You suspect cutaneous leishmaniasis and have tciken a biopsy for both histology and culture. Which of the following leishmaniasis species causes visceral leishmanisis only with no cutaneous lesions?
questions.explanation:
Lelshmaniasisdonovani is the only leishmaniasis species tilat causes visceral leishmaniasis and typically presents with pancytopenia and splenomegaly due to involvement of both the spleen and bone marrow.
All other leishmaniasis species give cutaneous lesions that are div,ded into new and old world cutaneous leishmaniasis.
Old world cutaneous leishmaniasis is due to L.tropica, L.major, L.ethiopica and L.in fantum.
New world leishmaniasis is due to L.brasiliensis and L.mexicana. "' L.brasiliensis can result in mucosal involvement.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding cat scratch disease is incorrect?
options: Bartonellosis is the disseminated form of the infection in the im munocompromised host.
Bacillary angiomatcsis is the cutaneous-limited manifestation of Bartonella henselae.
Lymphadenopathy may occur in half of the cases.
The condition is self-limiting in immunocompetents and therefore conservative management is appropriate.
The responsible organism is Bartonella henselae.
questions.explanation:
Lymphadenopathy is found in 100% of cases of cat suatch disease.
The condition is common in children and presents with a papulo-pustular eruption with scratch marks, mostly on the hands.
Azithromycin has been used in some cases but no treatment is required in immunocompetent individuals.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old patient develops an expanding rash on her left thigh after a tick bite. If untreated she is has a highest risk of developing:
questions.explanation:
Erythema chronlcum migrans is seen in 60-90% of patients diagnosed with Lyme disease.
If untreated, approximately 60% of patients will go on to have oligoarticular arthritis (usually the knee).
Approximately 10% develop a neurologic manifestation such as facial nerve palsy.
Approximately 5% develop a cardiac complication such as varying degrees of atrioventricular block).

questions.stem: The second member of a family who have recently installed a hot-tub in their back garden presents to your clinic with follicular-based papules and pustules predominantly distributed over the torso, buttocks and legs. What is the most probable causative agent?
questions.explanation:
The number of privately owned hut-tubs in the UK is estimated at 100,000 and is rising.
In turn, cases of hot-tub folliculitis - a condition caused by the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeroginosa and thought to arise from inadequate chlorination - are also increasing.
Diagnosis is largely clinical, with a predominantly truncal eruption appearing within a few days of exposure to contaminated water.
Typically, the condition is self-limiting and requires no treatment. Extensive disease, especially in immunosuppressed individuals, may necessitate anti-gram negative systemic therapy.

questions.stem: A haematology colleague asks for your opinion on a 38-year-old female, with newly-diagnosed lupus-related leukopaenia, who now presents with pearly umbilicated papules over her breasts and hands. Her otherwise well 11-month old child has crops of similar lesions. What is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Molluscumcontagiosum is a DNA poxvirus, as is Orf virus
Diagnosis of SLE is based on a combination of clinical findings and laboratory evi den,:e. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) uses a standard diagnostic classification requiring at least 4 out of the following 11 criteria to be met: Matar rash, discoid rash. photosensitivity, oral ulcers, non-erosive arthritis, pleuritis or pericarditis, renal dysfunction, neurological dysfunction, haematological disorder (such as leukopaenia), immunological disorder and positive antinuclear antibody.

questions.stem: A middle-aged business man who travels extensively abroad has a monomorphic follicular eruption over the face and trunk. Diagnostic skin biopsy demonstrates a dense eosinophilic peri-follicular infiltrate. He denies taking any prescription, overthe-counter or herbal remedies. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Eosinophilic folliculitis is a feature of cell-mediated immunodeficiency, although nc definitive infective aetiology has been identified.
With HIV infection it is seen when the CD4 lymphocyte count falls below 300 cells/ mm3 and typically improves with Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy.
Papuloerythroderma of Ofuji or "Ofuji disease" is a variant of eosinophilic folliculitis that is typically found in Japan and is not associated with immunodeficiency.
PQ.7.63

questions.stem: A 55-year patient with a history of self-neglect and features of malnutrition is admitted with an infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease necessitating systemic steroids. On day 7 of admission he develops haemorrhagic bullae over h;s buttocks, groins and inner thighs that break do11,n to leave deep purulent ulcers. Which causative agent would you expect to identify on blood culture?
questions.explanation:
Ecthyma gangrenosum results from haematogenous spread of infective agents.
Pseudomonas aeriginosa is the most common cause but all those listed c.an be causal agents.
Fungal infections such as Aspergillosis, Candida and Zygomycosis may also cause ecthyma gangrenosum.
It usually occurs in immune-compromised or severely unwell patients.
Characteristic lesions concern haemorrhagic pustules that evolve into deep necrotic ulcers.

questions.stem: A GP refers a 17-year-old veterinary nurse trainee with suspected Catch Scratch Disease. If her suspicion is correct, what is the likelihood that the patient with have lympadenopathy?
questions.explanation:
Catch scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae.
Localised, tender lymphadenopathy occurs distal to theiteofa bite or scratch 1-3 weeks after inoculation.
A discrete papule or vesicle may also be seen at the site of Inoculation.
Approximately SO% patients experience systemic symptoms such as fever, headache and malaise.
In immunocompetent individuals, the infection is self-limiting, with conservative management appropriate.
immunocompromised patients, however, are at significant risk of developing com plications such as bacillary angiomatosis (a vascular lesion that may extend from the skin and soft tissue into underlying to bone) and require treatment with antimicrobials such as azithromycin.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presented with a three month history of asymptomatic generalized maculopapular eruption, on his trunk and extremities. He also had some small, smooth grey patches on his tongue and has been complaining of headaches for four weeks. Further questioning revealed a recent history of unprotected sexual intercourse. Which of the following statements in this condition is correct?
options: Argyll-Robertson pupil is a common finding.
Histology often shows parakeratosis, lichenoid changes and erythrocyte extravasation in the absence of plasma cells.
Potential adverse reactions occurring within the first 24 hours of therapy include headache, myalgia and worsening of the eruption.
Response to Penicillin is generally very poor.
questions.explanation:
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute febrile reaction that can occur within the first 24 hours of therapy of secondary syphilis.
Syphilis responds very well to treatment with penicillin.
Dark field microscopy is often of limited value in oral lesions due to the presence of saprophytic spirochetes in the oral cavity.
Pupillary constriction with convergence accommodation but no reaction to strong light describes Argyll-Robertson pupils which is a feature of tertiary syphilis.
Histologically, secondary syphilis is characterised by a superficial and deep peri-vascular infiltrate containing plasma cells.

questions.stem: Borreli:;i borgderfori has been linked to the pathogenesis of all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Rocky mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and can present with a maculo-papular eruption around the wrists and ankles which may become haemorrhagic and purpuric.
Marginal zone B cell lymphoma has been associated with Borrelia in Europe and pa tients ore often screened for this infelition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with black, necrotic palatal ulceration in insulin-dependent diabetics with poor diabetic control?
questions.explanation:
Rhinocerebral form of zygomycosis is associated with black, necrotic, palatal ulceration.
It is associated with poorly controlled insulin-dependent diabetes and keto-acidosis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old East Timorian immigrant presents with multiple numerous, variable-sized erythematous and dusky annular macules, ill-defined patches and well-demarcated plaques scattered across the trunk, arms, proximal legs and the face. He complains of hand and feet numbness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Diagnosis of leprosy is primarily clinical and is based on presence of one of following three features-hypopigmented or erythematous patches with definite loss of sensation, thickened peripheral nerves and acid-fast bacilli on skin smears or biopsy material.
Histology is the gold standard for diagnosis of leprosy.
Identification of endoneuritis (nerve disruption and fragmentation) which can be difficult on haematoxylin and eosin is helped by S100 stain which enables differentiation of tuberculoid leprosy from other cutaneous granulomatous diseases.

questions.stem: Which of the following is thought to be secondary to mycobacterium tuberculosis infection?
questions.explanation:
Erythema induratum of Bazin and nodular vasculitis describe the most common form of lobular panniculitis with vasculitis.
The term erythema induratum of Bazin is used for cases in which an aetiologic relationship with tuberculosis is demonstrated.
Presents as erythematous subcutaneous nodules and plaques on the posterior as pectsof the lower legs, which may ulcerate and heal with scarring,
Polymerase chain reaction may demonstrate mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA in skin biopsy specimens of patients with erythema induratum of Bazin.
A full course of anti-tuberculosis triple-agent therapy should be Instituted when mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA Is isolated.
Other therapeutic measures include potassium iodide, supporting bandages, bed rest, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with "leopard skin" pattern of depigmentation?
questions.explanation:
Several infections can result in pigmentary changes in the skin.
Onchocercaldepigmentation or "leopard skin" is the commonest feature of onchocerciasis and is rarely associated with pruritus.
It presents as hypopigmented patches with peri-follicular spots of normally pigmented skin, typically on the pre-tibial area of older people in endemic areas.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man presented with a maculo-papular eruption on the trunk with inguinal lymphadenopathy and a painless penile ulcer. History reveals that he had unprotected sexual intercourse few months before the onset of eruption. Darkfield microscopy showed the presence of treponemas. In the absence of any allergies, the first-line antibiotic in this condition is:
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis in this case is secondary syphilis with primary chancre and should al ways be considered in the differential of a painless genital ulcer (chancre).
Secondary syphilis can present as maculo-papular eruption which typically involves the palms.
Other conditions that result in macular palmar involvement are HIV-seroconversion and erythema multiforme.
Penicillins are the first-line treatment in syphilis.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presented to the dermatologist with a 3-month history of progressive development of bald patches on the scalp, with pruritus and some discharging areas. On examination, there were scaly patches of alopecia with some pustules and broken hairs. Wood's light examination showed positive fluorescence. The parents report that they keep pets at home. What is the most likely organism in this case?
questions.explanation:
The history here is highly suggestive of a zoophilic dermatophyte infection of which Microsporum canis is the commonest.
The commonest sources of microsporum canis are cats and dogs.
Trichophyton verrucosum is also a zoophilic species; however, this is often found in cattle and infected patients develop a very inflammatory kerion-like inflammation.
Trichophyton tonsurans and Trichophyton rubrum are both anthropophilic (human to human spread), and do not fluoresce under Wood's light.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl returned back from a visit to Connecticut, USA, where she was visiting her relatives. She was complaining of a slightly pruritic erythematous rash in tr lower leg, which seemed to be expanding, though on further questioning she recalls being bitten by an insect whilst on a picnic. What is the most appropriate antibiotic of choice in this case?
questions.explanation:
The history and clinical examination point towards a diagnosis of erythema annulare centrifugum / Lyme's disease secondary to tick bite.
These ticks are commonly found in some areas of the world. The name Lyme, relates to a town in Conn.:cticut where these cases were first reported.
Although doxycycline would be the treatment of choice, this would be contra-;ndi cated in view of patient's age.
Amoxicillin would be the second choice in the absence of penicillin allergy.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl is seen in your clinic with fever and a rash. On examination of the oral mucosa, Forschheimer spots are seen. W at are Forschheimer spots a feature of?
questions.explanation:
Forlichheimer spots are small erythematous macules on the palate seen in Rubella (German measles).
They are not a feature of congenital rubella.
White "Koplik" spots are characteristic of measles.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old atopic patient is admitted with eczema herpeticum. Eczema herpeticum can complicate all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Eczema herpeticum is the presence of disseminated herpes in the setting of underlying skin diseases (most commonly, atopic eczema).
Besides atopic eczema, eczema herpeticum has also been associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis, Darier's disease, pemphigus vulgaris, mycosis fungoides, WiskottAldrich disease, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, and second degree burns.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old Nigerian man presents with a solitary hyperpigmentedirregular macule on the palmar surface of the hand. Microscopy of skin scrapings treated with 20% KOH reveal thick, septate, branching hyphae that contain a dark pigment in their walls. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Tinea nigra is an uncommon superficial dermatomycosis usually caused by Hortaeawerneckll which is classified in the family Dematiaceae.
Tinea nigra appears as a hyperpigmented macule, which usually occurs on the palms.
Tinea nigra is a superficial mycosis of the stratum corneum.
Infection is believed to occur as a result of inoculation from a contaminated source such as soil, sewage, wood, or compost.
Microscopic examination of skin scrapings treated with 20% KOH reveals thick, septate, branching hyphae that contain a dark pigment in their walls.
Topical application of antifungal agents e.g. clotrimazole or ketoconazole usually lead to resolution of tinea nigra within 2-4 weeks.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old farmer was admitted with multiple nodules on the left leg in a sporotrichoid pattern. Gram stain of the clinical specimen showed thin, gram-positive branching filamentous bacteria, weakly positive with acid-fast staining. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Nocardiosis is caused by aerobic Gram-positive filamentous bacteria.
It has a worldwide distribution, and is an environmentally acquired infection, due to primary traumatic inoculation.
Pulmonary infections are mostly seen in immunocompromised patients and skin infections mostly in immunocompetent patients.
Skin diseases are mostly caused by N. brasiliensis and less commonly N. asteroldes, N. otidiscaviarum, and N. farcinica.
Cutaneous nocardiosis occurs either as cellulitis or more characteristic lymphocutaneousncdules in a sporotrichoid pattern.
Skin lesions also occur in disseminated disease.
Diagnosis is based on Gram stain of clinical specimen which shows thin, gram-positive branching bacteria, weakly positive with acid-fast staining.
Microbiologic isolation of Nocardia sp. is diagnostic, but requires keeping cultures under observation for 5 to 7 days.
Treatment of choice is sulfonamides.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old Asian man is admitted with painful and tender, bright-pink, dermal and subcutanem;s nodules. He is febrile and anorexic. He has been receiving anti leprosy treatment. Which of the following subtypes of leprosy was the most likely primary diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Erythema nodosum leprosum (type II reaction) occurs most often in lepromatous leprosy (75%).
It may occur before, during, or after chemotherapy.
The median time of onset is almost 1 year after onset of treatment.
It is characterized by crops of painful and tender bright-pink, dermal and subcutaneous nodules arising in clinically normal skin., in association with fever, anorexia, and malaise.
Arthralgia and arthritis are commonly seen.
Neuritis, adenitis, orchitis/epididymitis or iritis, may rarely be the initial presentation.
A neutrophilic leukocytosisis seen.
Thalidomide is the treatment of choice.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old returning traveler presents with a creeping eruption on her foot. All of the following are recognized treatments for this eruption except:
questions.explanation:
Cut;meous larva migrans infection results in a creeping eruption that occurs when the larvae of dog or cat hookworm (Ankylostoma duodenale and Ankylostoma bra zliense) penetrate intact, exposed skin and begin migrating through the epidermis.
This gives rise to tingling/prickling at the site of exposure within 30 minutes of penetration of the larvae.
Pruritic, erythematous, linear, serpiginious advancingiesions track 3-4 cm from the penetration site.
Thiabendazole is the agent of choice in cutaneous larva migrans.
Topical application is used for early, localized lesions.
The oral route is preferred for widespread eruption.
Other effective alternative treatments include oral albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has proximal subungual onychomycosis. Which of the following underlying illnesses should be excluded in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Proximal subungual onychomycosis is an uncommon variant of dermatophyte infec tion caused by T. rubrum and is often related to intercurrent disease.
Paronychia is not a feature.
immunosuppressed patients, especially those who are human immunodeficiency vi rus-positive, may present with proximal subungual onychomycosis.
Other associations of proximal subungual onychomycosis include peripheral vascular disease and diabetes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the commonest variant of onychomycosis?
questions.explanation:
Onychomycosis is classified clinically as distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis (DLSO), superficial white onychomycosis (SWO), proximal subungual onychomycosis (PSO), candidal onychomycosis and total dystrophic onychomycosis.
Of these, distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis is the commonest and is most commonly caused by T. rubrum.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presented with an intensely pruritic follicular eruption on the fac,eind trunk which has not responded to oral flucloxacillin and topical anti-fungal tr rapy given to him in the community. A swab from a follicular pustule showed no growth and a biopsy showed a dense eosinophilic perifollicular infiltrate. The diagnosis of eosinophilic folliculitis was made. Which of the following conditions should he be investigated for?
questions.explanation:
HIV infection can have many dermatological manifestations and a diagnosis of eosinophilic folliculitis should be considered in any HIV patient who presents with a pruritic sterile folliculitis in which the biopsy shows an eosinophilic inflammatory cell infiltrate.
There are 3 types of eosinophilic folliculitis; HIV-associated, classic type (also called Ofuji syndrome) and the infancy-associated type.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old diabetic presents with an asymptomatic erythematous rash on both axillae. Wood's light examination shows coral red fluorescence. Which chemical is responsible for this fluorescence?
questions.explanation:
Erythrasma is caused by the Gram positive bacterium Corynebacterium minutissi mum.
The patches of erythrasma display coral red fluoresence on Wood's lamp examination.
This is secondary to coproporphyrin III production by Corynebacterium minutissi mum.

questions.stem: A 6-week old baby presented with multiple papules, pustules and closed comedones on both cheeks. Examination of the rest of the skin was unremarkable and he was otherwise a healthy neonate. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Neonatal acne consists of both inflammatory lesions and comedones.
It presents in the first three months of life.
This occurs due to the presence of the maternal hormones which stimulate the sebaceous glands In the neonate.
The condition resolves spontaneously without treatment in the first three months of life.
Neonatal cephalic pustulosis is a pustular condition mainly affecting the head of neonates, without comedones. This is may be due to overgrowth of various Malassezia species.
Infantile acne appears after the age of three months and is more common in boys due to higher levels of testosterone in the first 6-12 months of life.
There may be a positive family history, and the condition includes bothinflammatory and comedonal lesions, however often inflammatory lesions predominate and in severe cases, cystic acne may occur.
Children with infantile acne should be evaluated with an endocrinological screening for underlying abnormalities, and there may be a risk for severe acne later in life.
Staphylococcal pustulosis presents with diffuse pustules in the absence of comedones, on the trunk and limbs.

questions.stem: What is the inheritance pattern for incontinentia pigmenti?
questions.explanation:
incontinentia pigmenti is a genodermatosisthat primarily affects females asmales do not survive this X-linked dominant disorder, unless they are mosaic. The commonest mutation involves a deletion in the NEMO gene on the long arm of the X chromosome.
The condition has four stages; inflammatory vesicular stage which tends to be along Blaschko's lines, a verrucous stage, hyperpigmented, and finally hypopigmented stage in which whorls and swirls develop in a characteristic "Chinese letter" pattern.
There is associated ectodermal dysplasia and nail changes may occur including onycholysis, onychodystrophy and subungual hyperkeratosis.
Systemic defects can occur, and in particular, brain and eye involvement.
Patients with incontinentia pigmenti should have neurological and ophthalmic assessment.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old patient presents with multiple skin tags and skin-coloured papules on the face and neck. She has previously been admitted on three occasions for spontaneous pneumothoraces. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome manifests as fibrofolliculomas, trichodiscomas and acrochordons.
This is an autosomal dominant disorder and can be associated with renal and pulmonary cysts; and can present with pneumothoraces.
Rombo syndrome presents with basal cell carcinomas, trichoepitheliomas, hypotrichosis, atrophoderma and telangiectasia.
Bazex-Dupre-Christol syndrome presents with basal cell carcinomas, follicular at,ophoderma, pill torti, scrotal tongue, spiny hyperkeratosis, and neuropsychiat;'ic symptoms. It is an X-linked dominant disorder.
Gorlin's syndrome presents with basal cell carcinomas, palmo-plantar pits, odonto genic jaw cysts, frontal bossing, ovarian carcinoma / fibroma, medulloblastomas, lipomas, and epidermal cysts.
It is an autosomal dominant disorder due to PTCH1gene defect.

questions.stem: Which of the following genodermatoses is inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion?
questions.explanation:
Conradi-Hunermann syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern.
Patients are often born with a collodion-like membrane followed by an ichthyosiform erythroderma in Blaschko's lines.
There may also be follicular atrophodermc, scarring alopecia, scoliosis and cataracts.
Sjogren-Larsson syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder presents with ichthyosis at birth with spastic paralysis and mental retardation.
Netherton's syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder that presents with an exfoliative ery1:hroderma with ichthyosis lineariscircumflexa; the typical double edged migratory scale.
The typir.al feature is the so-called "bamboo" hairs showing microscopically the typ· ical trichorrhexis invaginata.
Lamellar ichthyosis presents with a collodion baby at birth. It is an autosomal recessive disorder.
Most patients develop later in life features of ectropion, inverted ears, plate-like scale, which is often "dirty brown", and palmo-plantar keratoderma.
Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disorder.

questions.stem: A 5-month old boy presented with a 6-week history of multiple tense vesicles and bullae appearing on the face, abdomen and scrotum.
