These arepainless and some are arranged in an annular configuration resembling a "crown of jewels''. No mucosal involvement is present and a biopsy showed a subepidermal bulla with dense neutrophilic infiltrate. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is true?
options: Histology typically shows a dense eosinophilic infiltrate.
Systemic corticosteroids are the first-line treatment of choice.
The disease is very rare in children.
questions.explanation:
Linear IgA disease is the commonest bullous disorder in children.
Mucous membrane involvement may occur in half of the patients.
Dapsone remains the first-line treatment of choice.
Subepidermal Infiltrate is predominantly neutrophilic.
Drugs can cause a similar disease in adults (drug-induced linear IgA disease) with vancomycin being the commonest.
Other vesiculo-bullous disorders in childhood include: congenital HSV, congenital varicella, bullous impetigo, scabies, toxic epidermal necrolysis, staphylocoocal scalded skin syndrome, thermal burns, incontinentia pigmenti, epidermolysis bullosa, neonatal pemphigus vulgaris (from the mother), bullous pemphigoid, bullous mastocytosis and bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma.

questions.stem: Which of the following inherited forms of epidermolysis bullosa is associated with mutations of the gene coding for type VII collagen (COL7Al)?
questions.explanation:
Epidermolysis bullosa simplex-mutation in Keratins 5/14.
Hemi-desmosomal epidermolysis bullosa- Epidemolysis bullosa with muscular dystrophy-mutation in PLEC1, EB with pyloric atresia-mutation in ITGB4/ITGA6.
Junctional epidermolysis bullosa-mutation in LAMB3/LAMA3/LAMG2.
Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa-mutation in COL7Al.
Kindler syndrome-mutation in KINDl.
Ectodermal dysplasla-skin fragility-mutation in PKPl.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old Caucasian boy is referred to the Paediatric dermatology clinic with the appearance of akinky, wavy hair on the scalp. You carry out hair pluck test and find tightly coiled hair on microscopy. Which other system involvement is to be excluded?
questions.explanation:
Woolly hair is the presence of kinl-.y, wavy hair on the scalp of persons of non-African or Negroid background.
Microscopically, the hairs are tightly coiled.
The unruly hair presents at birth or in infancy, usually as a solitary problem inherit d in an autosomal dominant fashion.
Mutations in the genes for the desmosomal proteins plakoglobin (Naxos disease) or desmoplakin give rise to the triad of woolly hair, striate palmar-plantar keratoderma, and cardiomyopathy.
Both recessive and dominant patterns of inheritance have been reported.
Assessment of cardiac status should be performed In all children presenting with generalized woolly hair.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient with Darier's disease present wich some changes affecting the fingernails. You expect to see some or all of the changes expect:
questions.explanation: Key features of nail disease in Darier's disease include longitudinal erythronychia, longitudinal leukonychia associated with distal nail plate nicking (V-shaped), and subungual hyperkeratotic papules.

questions.stem: Collodion baby" is a clinical finding describing a new-born infant encased in an oily parchment-like shiny skin. This finding can occur in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Collodion membranes may resolve spontaneously or evolve into non-bullous ichthysioform erythroderma or lamellar ichthyosis.
Complications m;;;y include infections, dehydration and hypernataemia.
Newborns with Netherton's syndrome typically present with an exfoliative erythroderma.
- Hay-Wells syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition wliich is a type of ectodermal dysplasia caused by a mutation in the TP7PQL gene.
The 2 features that differentiate Hay-Wells syndrome from other ectodermal dysplasias are the occurence of "clefting" of the lip or palate and the fusion of the edges (often become fibrotic) of the upper and lower eyelids.

questions.stem: A 3-month old preterm boy is admitted with a few w ek history of scaling and vesicular eruption in the peri-oral and acral distribution. The child is Irritable and has been having diarrhoea for 4 weeks. What is the most likely cause of these symptoms7
questions.explanation:
Acrodermatitis enteropathlca may be autosomal recessive or acquired.
It is caused by deficiency of zinc.
Scaling and vesicles in a perl-orificial and acral distribution are common.
Diarrhoea is often present.
At risk population includes premature infants, aicoholics and patients with absorption defects.
Zinc replacement brings about rapid improvement.

questions.stem: A 14-week-old girl is referred with a 12-week history of a rapidly enlarging bruise-like swelling of the left upper eyelid completely obscuring the left eye. Examination shows a large haemangioma filling the left upper eyelid and orbit, completely closing the eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Oral propranolol has replaced oral corticosteroids as the mainstay of treatment for high risk haemangiomas including those that risk loss of vision.
It should also be considered for subglottic or nasal haemangiomas or rapidly enlarging haemangiomas.

questions.stem: A-12 week old boy has an enlarging tender ulcerated haemangioma on the perine'31 area. Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Becaplermln 0.01% gel is the mainstay treatment.
Intralesional steroids are the treatment of choice.
Potent topical corticosteroids are usually ineffective.
Pulsed dye laser is ineffective for pain control.
Spontaneous resolution is unlikely in perineal haemangioma.
questions.explanation:
Pulsed-dye laser is effective for treating ulcerated hemangiomas and can result in pain reduction, rapid re-epithelialization, and hastened involution.
There is a small risk of worsening of ulceration with pulsed dye laser.
Pulsed dye laser is not used routinely in the treatment of uncomplicated haemangiomas.
Long pulsed and frequency-doubled Nd:YAG lasers may also be used to treat ulcer ated haemangiomas.
Topical imiquimod cream, becaplermin 0.01% gel and oral propranol have all been used successfully in the treatment of infantile haemangiomas.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with dry scaly skin since birth. Examination shows dark, polygonal, firmly adherent scales on the posterior neck, upper trunk, and extensor surfaces of the extremities. He has a history of cryptorchidism. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
X-linked ichthyosis is caused by deficiency of the enzyme steroid sulfatase (STS).
The scaling is mildin the first few days of life and gives way to dark brown, polygonal, firmly adherent scales.
Palms and soles are usually spared.
During late childhood the rash becomes more prominent on the trunk and extremities, particularly on the extensor surfaces of the legs.
Corneal opacities may be seen in patients and carriers.
Cryptorchidism occurs in 20% of patients.

questions.stem: A 14-week-old girl was referred with a 12-week history of a rapidly enlarging bruise-like swelling of the left upper eyelid completelv obscuring the left eye. She had repeated episodes of fresh rectal bleeding. Examination shows a large haemangioma filling the left upper eyelid and orbit. Computerised tomographic scan of abdomen shows a large haemangioma in the right lobe of the liver and extensive small intestinal haemangiomas. Which of the following most likely describes the condition?
questions.explanation:
PHACES syndrome is a neurocutaneous syndrome representing a spectrum of anomalies in which segmental haemangiomas, most commonly of the face, are associated with one or more of: posterior fossa brain malformations, arterial anomalies, coarctation of the aorta and cardiac defects, and eye abnormalities (PHACES if ventral developmental defects such as sternalclefting and/or supraumbilicalraphe are included).
The most common manifestations noted are structural and arterial anomalies of the brain, followed by cardiac anomalies and/or coarctation of the aorta, eye abnormalities, and ventral developmental defects. The most commonly reported sites for visceral haemangiomas among such patients are the brain and mediastinum.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with erosions under her breasts and axillae. Her mother had similar S'ymptoms which were treated as flexural psoriasis. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?
options: Direct immunofluoresence shows IgG and C3 deposition at dermo-epidermal junction.
Kaposi's varicelliform eruption is a recognised complication.
The defect is identified on ATP2C1gene.
White bands on the fingernails may be seen.
questions.explanation:
Hailey-Hailey disease (familial chronic benign pemphigus) is an autosomal dominant disorder with incomplete penetrance.
Approximately one thirds of patients do not have a family history of the disorder.
The defect appears to be in a calcium pump protein, ATP2Cl which encodes the secretory pathway Ca2+/Mn2 ATPase (hSPCAl).
Patients present with crusts and vesicles studded on erythematous plaques in flexural areas including the genital infra-mammary region, neck, and axillae.
Longitudinal leukonychia may be seen on fingernails.
Treatment is aimed at suppressing symptoms and includes anti-perspirants, antibacterials, topical steroids and immunosuppressives in recalcitrant cases.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old Pakistani girl was referred with a long-standing history of general stiffening of the tongue with the presence of beaded papules on the eyelids and on the peri-orbital skin and hoarseness of her voice. There are also verrucous-like plaques on the elbows and knuckles, in addition to dental anomalies. Further history reveals that her older sister, aged 16, suffers from the same condition. The inheritance pattern of this condition is?
options: An acquired condition therefore not inherited.
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis here is lipoid proteinosis which is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterised by the above signs and symptoms.
It is caused by a mutation of the gene ECN-1.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy presented with targetoid large erythematous macules with purpura and oedema on his limbs and face. History reveals that the baby suffered an upper respiratory tract infection ten days prior to the appearaniie of this rash. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is true?
options: ANCA level must be checked immediately.
Histology will show leukocytoclastic vasculitis and the condition will resolve spontaneously.
Histology will show multiple thrombi in the superficial vessels.
The condition has a very poor prognosis and rapid initiation of corticosteroid therapy is required.
Treatment with hyperoaric oxygen is required.
questions.explanation:
Acute haemorrhagic oedema of infancy can occur following upper respiratory tract infection and clinically presents with targetoid-like purpuric macules associated with oedema.
The condition is transient, has an excellent prognosis and no treatment is required other than supportive measures.
Histologically, the lesions show small vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis and occasion ally IgA deposition in the vessels.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl presents with a persistent eczematous eruption covering her face, trunk and limbs which is associated with coarse facial features, doughy skin and broad nasal bridge. She also has a history of recurrent fractures and poor dentition. She has been found to have persistently raised eosinophil count, significantly raised IgE levels but no demonstrable specific igEs against any particular allergen. On examination, you also note that she has a high-arched palate. Mutation of which gene is responsible for thiscondition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features and lab abnormalities here are consistent with the diagnosis of hyper-lgEsyndrome.
The autosomal dominant variant is related to STAT3 defects; however the autosomal recessive variant is related to lYK2 defects.
Other features of this disease are recurrent pyogenic infections, asthma, hyper-ex tensible joints, scoliosis and neurological complications.

questions.stem: Which of the following structural hair abnormalities can be seen in Netherton's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Trichorrhexis invaginata is also called "bamboo hair" and is found in Netherton's syndrome.
Increased fragility of the hair shaft is also seen in monilethnx, trichorrhexis nodosa, trichothiodystrophy and pill torti.
In loose anagen syndrome and woolly hair, the hair shafts are not fragile.

questions.stem: which of the following sub-types of morphea is the commonest in children?
questions.explanation:
Linear nicrphea can be associated with joint symptoms and is the commonest subtype in children.
The plaque type of morphea is thecommonest in adults.
En coup de Sabre sub-type of morphea on the head can be associated with ocular and neurological abnormalities.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old man presented with diffuse asymptomatic angiokeracomas on the trunk and genitalia with bilateral leg oedema. In addition he has been complaining of neuropathic pains in his limbs and hypohidrosis. Urinalysis showed evidence of proteinuria. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?
options: Cardiac arrhythmias are a potential complication in this condition.
The angiokeratomas tend not to respond to enzyme replacement therapy.
The disease is generaliy milder in women.
The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant.
questions.explanation:
Fabry's disease is an X-linked recessive disorder.
Female carriers can still manifest the disease but it tends to be milder.
The angiokeratomas and lymphoedema generally do not respond to enzyme replacement therapy.
Hypohidrosis and neuropathic pain crises are other manifestations of the disease.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a history of thyroid carcinoma and multiple facial tricholemmomas presented with cobblestoning of the oral mucosa and palmo-plantar keratoses. The most likely diagnosis here is:
questions.explanation:
The rare Cowden's syndrome should be suspected when a patient presents with oral cobblestoning, palmo-plantar keratoses, tricholemmomas and ahistory of internal malignany (mostly breast, thyroid or uterus).
Muir-Torre syndrome can also be associated with internal malignancies but the cuta neous manifestations are of sebaceous tumours or eruptive keratoacanthomas.
Gardner's syndrome is associated with polyposis coli (risk of colon carcinoma) and multiple epidermoid cysts and/or lipomas.
Bazex syndrome is also called acrokeratosisparaneoplastica and is a paraneoplastic phenomenon that often presents with a psoriasiform appearance of the hands and feet accentuated around the nails with associated nail changes, palmo-plantar keratoderma and alopecia.

questions.stem: Dental anomalies can be found in all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
In Netherton's syndrome there is ichthyosis with hair shaft defects but dental abnormalities are not a feature.
Other conditions that can be associated with dental anomalies include ectodermal dysplasia, congenital erythropoietic porphyria, focal dermal hypoplasia, Sjogren- Larsson syndrome and Papillon-Lefevre syndrome.

questions.stem: An infant has a focal area of midline alopecia, overlying a blue-tinged compressible nodule, surrounded by long dark coarse hair. Which of the following investigations would you instigate?
questions.explanation:
Features described are those of the hair collar sign; a relatively specific marker of meningoceles and other types of cranial dysraphism.
CT or MRI imaging is necessary to determine whether an intracranial connection is present.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old amateur rugby player experiences considerable distress during a dental procedure despite receiving multiple local anaesthetic injections. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
There exists an increasingly well-recognised association between Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, specifically of the hypermobility type, and resistance to local anaesthetics.
This can necessitate a higher local anaesthetic dose, a greater time between delivering analgesia and starting surgery, or even consideration for general anaesthesia.
The underlying mechanism awaits full elucidation.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is noted to have exaggerated wrinkling of the palms after brief immersion in water. Which of the following investigations would you instigate?
questions.explanation:
Aquagenic wrinkling of the palms is a cutaneous manifestation of cystic fibrosis that may also be seen in carriers of cystic fibrosis gene mutations.
It usually presents with translucent papules that coalesce to form oedematous plaques.
Time-to-onset·is typically a few minutes, but is usually longer in carriers of cystic fibrosis mutations.
The exact cause isunclear and most authorities agree that it is related to dysfunction in sweating.
Reported treatments include topical aluminium preparations and botulinum toxin injections.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy, whose family have recently moved to the UK, presents with crops of reddish-brown pigmented plaques and papillomatous lesions over his face, trunk and limbs. These first appeared aged 12 and have steadily grown more extensive. A diagnosis of epidermodysplasia verruciformis is suspected. This disorder results from mutation in which gene?
questions.explanation:
Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (or Lewandowsky-Lutz dysplasia) is a rare disorder, typically inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion.
Mutations in EVER 1 or 2 genes result in defective cell-mediated immunity.
Patients are predisposed to HPV infection and squamous cell carcinoma.
Numerous HPV serotypes are associated, although not HPV 16.
HPV 5, 8, 10, and 47 serotypes have been isolated in over 90% of epidermodysplasia verruciformis-associated squamous cell carcinomas.

questions.stem: Bart-Pumphrey syndrome results from mutation in the gene encoding connexin 26. The function of which structures will be affected?
questions.explanation:
Bart-Pumphrey syndrome is characterised by the clinical triad of prominent knuckle pads, leuconychia and deafness.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive and arises from mutation in the GJB2/connexin 26 gene.
Other disorders resulting from mutation inconnexin 26 include Palmoplantar Keratoderma with Deafness and Vohwinkel syndrome.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl is seen in clinic with multiple lentigines and blue naevi. During examination, you also elicit a cardiac murmur leading you to suspect an underlying diagnosis of LAMB. To what does the 'A' in this acronym refer?
questions.explanation:
LAMB (Lentigines, Atrial Myxomas, Mucocutaneous Myxomas, Blue Naevi) is a type of Myxoma syndrome.
Other recognised disorders on this disease spectrum are NAME (naevi, atrial myxomas, rnyxoidneurofibroma, and ephelides) and carney syndrome (atrial, cutaneous and mammary myxomas, lentigines, blue naevi, endocrine disorders and testicular tumours).
Myxoma syndrome may be autosomal dominant or sporadic.
One implicated gene in familial cases is PRKARlA, a cell cycle regulator.

questions.stem: You have been reviewing an 18-month year old boy with multiple papules over his cheeks and forehead. Initially lesions appeared smooth and pink but lately have developed a yellowish appearance. Diagnostic skin biopsy is consistent with juvenile xanthogranuloma. What action might you consider?
options: None of the above - this is a skin-limited disorder.
questions.explanation:
Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a type of non-langerhan's cell histiocytosis.
it is most commonly seen in male children but can oc.cur in both sexes at any age.
Its cause is unknown and diagnosis is confirmed by skin biopsy with collections of, often foamy, lipid-full histiocytes seen in the dermis.
There is no associated dyslipidaemia.
Ophthalmic involvement, however, can be associated with spontaneous hyphema leading to secondary glaucoma and blindness. Those at greatest risk are children younger than 2 years with multiple skin lesions

questions.stem: You see a 2-month old child with scarring blistering of the skin. Other ieatures include a mitten deformity with proximal fusion or all hand and toes webs and aphonia. Which of the following combinations concerning 1) inheritance 2) protein(s) affected 3) cellular structure affected and 4) level of the blister, for thiscondition is true?
options: Autosomal recessive, collagen 7 (COL7A1), anchoring fibril, sublamlnal densa.
Autosomal recessive, laminin 332, anchoring filament, lamina-lucida split.
Autosomal dominant, collagen 7 (COL7Al), anchodng fibril, sublaminal densa.
Autosomal dominant, keratin 5 &14, intermediate filament, intra-epithelial split.
questions.explanation:
The clinical features described are those of the autosomal recessive, or Hallopeau-Siemans, type of dystrophic epidermolyis bullosa (EB).
Other features include enamel defects and dental caries, nail dystrophy and high propensity to squamous cell carcinoma.
Answer C relates to the autosomal dominant form of dystrophic EB, which is less severe and improves with age.
Answer B relates to junctional EB, classically subdivided into Herlitz and non-Herlitz types.
Answer D relates to EB simplex, which in turn can be subdivided into localised (Weber Cockayne), generalised (Dowling Meara) and superficial types.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl is referred to the department of paediatric dermatology with a port-wine stain overlying her right mid-back. She is under the neurology team for a radiculopathy. You suspect a unifying diagnosis of Cobb Syndrome. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Cobb syndrome (also known as Cutaneous Vertebral Medullary Angiomatosis or Spinal Arteriovenous Metameric Syndrome) is defined by coexistence of vascular malformations in all tissue layers of a segmental dermatome.
Venous or arteriovenous malformations over the back are present from birth may be the only clue to an underlying spinal cord AVM.
Neurological manifestations typically involve lower limb motor or sensory deficit and/or sphincter deficits.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old pregnant woman is seen in clinic with her fourth skin malignancy. There is strong family history of cancer with her father and paternal grandmother having suffered medulloblastoma and ovarian cancer, respectively. She and her partner, who has no personal or family of skin cancer, wish to know the likelihood that their child, which they know to be a daughter, will also be affected by the condition. Which of the following is the correct answer?
questions.explanation:
Gorlin's syndrome is inherited in an autosomal domirant fashion.
Non-basal cell carcinoma skin signs can include epidermal cysts, lipomas and palmoplantar cysts.
Bony manifestations include bifid ribs, frontal bossing and ontontogenic jaw cysts.
Other associated malignancies include medulloblastoma and ovarian cancer.

questions.stem: Whir.h of the following statements regards Naxos syndrome is most accurate?
options: It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the desmoplakin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy and striate PPK.
It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy and diffuse PPK.
It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and pre sents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and striate PPK.
It is autosomal dominant, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy and striate PPK.
It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and diffuse PPK.
questions.explanation:
Woolly hair may be an inherited as an isolated condition (usually in an autosomal dominant fashion) or as part of a syndrome (typically in an autosomal recessive fashion).
Answer A is true for Carvajal syndrome.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old healthy boy was born with a large purplish erythematous raised tumour with central telangiectasia surrounded by a pale halo on his left upper arm which did not increase in size in the first eight months of his life. At the age of one year, his mother noticed significant flattening of the lesion and fading of the halo. In this condition, which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: Central ulceration is a possible complication in the first few months of life.
Kasabach-Merritt syndrome occurs in some cases.
The histology is characterised by small capillary lobules surrounded by dense fibrous tissue with abnormally thin walled blood vessels in the centre.
This entity is characteristically negative to the immunoreactive glucose transporter-1 (GLUT-1).
Treatment with oral steroids should be commenced during the first three months of life.
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis here is rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma (RICH).
Central ulceration, calicification and Kasabach-Merritt syndrome may all occur in this entity.
Both RICH and non-involuting congenital haemangioma (NICH) are negative for GLUT- 1; as opposed to infantile haemangiomas that are positive to GLUT-1.
Both RICH and NICH are fully developed at birth unlike infantile haemangiomas.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient with Darier's disease is referred for evaluation of nail changes. Which of the following is not a recognized feature of nail disease in Darier's disease?
questions.explanation:
The nails in Darier's disease are fragile and split easily.
Other features include - combination of red and white longitudinal stripes (erytnroand leukonychia).
Distal V-shaped nick and subungual hyperkeratosis dre commonly seen.

questions.stem: In which of the following syndromes are multiple fibrofolliculomas a pathognomonic feature?
questions.explanation:
Fibrofolliculomas are tiny skin-colou;ed papules on the head, neck, and upper trunk.
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a mutation in the protein folliculin.
Salient features include fibrofolliculomas, trichodiscomas, and acrochordons.
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is associated with an increased risk of renal carcinomas and pneumothoraces.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the investigation of choice in fibromatosiscolli?
questions.explanation:
Fibromiltosiscolli (sterr.omastoid tumour of infancy) is a self-limiting benign proliferation of fibroblasts in the lower one-third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Presentation is in the first few weeks of life and the lesion can grow rapidly causing marked expansion of the sternocleidomastoid.
Clinical and radiographic differential diagnoses include rhabdomyosarcoma or neuroblastoma.
It is the most common cause of neonatal torticollis.
It usually resolves within the first year of life.
Excisional biopsy is not required except where malignancy is suspected.
Fine-needle aspiration is the preferred diagnostic technique and shows clusters of benign, spindled, plump fibroblasts with ovoid to elongated nuclei.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a feature of Conradi-Hi.inermann syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Conradi-Hunermann syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder.
Features include ichthyosiform scaling erythroderma patterned along the lines of Blaschko followed by bands of follicular atrophoderma, hyperpigmentation, cataracts, scarring alopecia, saddle-nose deformity, asymmetric limb reduction defects, and stippled calcifications of the epiphyses.
It is lethal in homozygous males.
Mutations occur in the emopamil binding protein gene at Xpll.23-pll.22.42.
ichthyosis, keratotic follicular plugging containing dystrophic calcification in newborns are also seen.

questions.stem: A neonate is born with distinctive features of harlequin ichthyosis. The gene defect is?
questions.explanation:
ATP2Cl is the gene defect in Hailey-Hailey disease.
The gene defect in lamellar ichthyosis is TGMl (transglut.;minase 1).
NEMO is the gene defect in incontinentia pigmenti and stands for NFKB Essential Modulator.

questions.stem: Cataracts are a feature of which of the following dermatological conditions?
questions.explanation:
Other conditions which can be associated with cataracts are Gorlin's syndrome, incontinentia pigmenti, Neurofibromatosis type-2, trichothiodystrophy, vitamin 812 deficiency, Werner's syndrome, Refsurn disease, Conradi-Hunermann syndrome, oral steroid use and PUVA therapy.
Beh et's disease can be associated with uveitis, retinal vasculitis and hypopyon.
Mucous membrane pemphigoid can cause symblepharon. ""Juvenile xanthogranulomas can be associated with glaucoma. "' Reiter's disease is associated with conjunctivitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following genes is defective in Darier's disease?
options: Calcium pump of the Golgi apparatus.
questions.explanation:
Darier's disease and Hailey-Hailey disease are acantholytic disorders.
Calcium pump of the sarco/ endoplasmic reticulum is defective in Darier's disease.
Defect in calcium pump of the Golgi apparatus results in Hailey-Hailey disease.
toss of function mutations in ATP2A2, which encodes sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) isoform 2 (SERCA2), a calcium pump transporting Ca2+ from the cytosol to the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum results in Darier's disease.

questions.stem: Defective calcium pump is not implicated in the pathogenesis of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Darier White disease, epidermal dyskeratotic acantholytic naevi (localized form of Darier disease caused by somatic mosaicism), and aAcrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf are caused by defects in the same gene encoding calcium pump of the endoplasmic reticulum.
Hailey-Hailey disease results from defective calcium pump of the Golgi apparatus.

questions.stem: Which ofthe following is not a feature of Piebaldism?
questions.explanation:
Piebaldism is caused by mutations in the KIT proto-oncogene.
Depigmented patches are present on the ventral or lateral trunk.
Hands and feet are spared.
Poliosis iscommon.
Deafness is not a feature.
Piebaldism with deafness is known as Woolf syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following subtypes of Waardenburg syndrome has Hirschsprung disease as an additional feature?
questions.explanation:
Waardenburg syndrome type 4, is caused by heterozygous mutations in the transcription factor gene SOXl0 or by homozygous mutations in the gene encoding the peptide ligand endothelln-3, EDN3, or its receptor, EDNRB.
These genes are important in melanocyte development and in the development of the distal aspect of enteric nervous system cells.
Waardenburg syndrome type 4 has features of Waardenburg syndrome type 1 (pig mentary abnormalities, dystopia canthorum, broadening of the nasal root, the presence of hypoplastic alae nasi, synophrys, poliosis, heterochromia irides, partial heterochromia irides, or hypoplastic blue irides, premature greying and congenital deafness).
In addition it is associated with Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionosis of the colon).

questions.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis is a clinical feature of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS) patients have oculocutaneous albinism with variable hypopigmentation of the skin, hair, and irides, and ocular abnormalities.
Additional features include lack of platelet dense bodies, prolonged bleeding time, mucous membrane bleeding, and a predisposition to epistaxis, easy bruising, and metromenorrhagia.
Pulmonary fibrosis is a common and severe manifestation of HPSl and HPS4.
Pulmonary fibrosis causes death between the fourth and sixth decades of life.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl presents with multiple skin coloured nodules on the skin. In addition she has numerous coffee-coloured patches and macules on her skin. Her mother has similar patches on her skin. You diagnose the condition as neurofibromatosis type 1. Which of the following is the earliest skin sign of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis-1are:
6 or more cafe-au-lait macules of >5 mm In greatest diameter in pre-puber tal children and >15 mr, i:1post-pubertal individuals.
2 or morP. neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform neurofibroma.
Freckling in axillary or inguinal regions.
2 or more Lisch nodules.
Optic gHomas.
Osseous lesions including sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of long bone cortex with or without pseudoarthrosis.
First degree relative with NF-1.
At least two of the above criteria should be present to make a diagnosis of NF-1.
Cafe-au-lait macules are sharply defined, light brown patches which may be present at birth or appear shortly after - noted in all children with NF-1by the age of 4 years.
Neurofibromas start to develop around puberty.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presents to the dermatolofy department as his parents have concerns about several lesions on his face and trunk which he has had for over a year. Clinically, these consisted of yellow to orange coloured small nodules. There was no history of erosions, blisters, or change in size following rubbing. The child is otherwise well in himself; there is no family history of such lesions. Which would be the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation:
Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a histiocytic disorder.
It presents In children as solitary yellow to orange coloured lesions.
Ophthalmic involvement is the most common extra-cutaneous site and should be considered in children with more than three lesions.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl was referred by the endocrinologists with a rash on the scalp and vulva. Examination shows extensive seborrhea on the scalp with some vesicular crusted lesions and erosions on the vulva. Erosions, purpura and ulceration were also seen on the lower back. She has been diagnosed with diabetes insipidus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Letterer-Siwe syndrome is the most severe form of Langerhan's cell histiocytosis.
Usually seen in children, it is associated with exuda'Cive, ulcerative seborrhoeic dermatitis-like eruption and systemic signs including hepatosplenomegaly.
Suspicion of the diagnosis should arise in any child with seborrhoeic dermatitis-like picture and the presence of petechieae.
- intertriginous lesions are common.
Loss of teeth may occur if mandiblular and maxillary bones are involved. "'Lymphadenopathy, bonemarrow involvement and thrombocytopaenia are also seen. "' Diabetes insipidus occurs secondary to involvement of the pituitary gland or hypothalamus.
Triad of proptosis, diabetes insipidus and skin rash are seen in Hand-Scholler- Christian disease.
The disease 1s commonly fulminnnt and fatal.
Vinblastine is the chemotherapeutic agent of choice.

questions.stem: A 6-month old girl is referred to the department of paediatric dermatology with a port-wine stain on the left side of her face. She is under the care of the neurologists for epilepsy. Which of the following best describes the Inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Sturge-Weber syndrome is a sporadic malformation of the vasculature of the leptomeninges, facial dermal capillaries and often ocular vessels.
It is characterized by facial port wine stain most commonly affecting areas innervated by the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
Homolateralleptomeningeal angiomatosis results in epilepsy in 75-90% of cases.

questions.stem: A 10-month old baby presented with an 8-month history of a progressively worsening eruption consisting of red-to-light brown patches and plaques on the truni, and limbs. His mother reported that some of them have blistered, particularly following gentle rubbing. Whilst in clinic you can elicit the Darier's sign on some of the plaques, which of the following should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is urticaria pigmentosa which is a form of cutaneous mastocytosis.
Drugs which can trigger histamine release from mast cells should be avoided and these include NSAIDs, aspirin, opiates, atropine, procaine and polymyxin B.
Other forms of cutaneous mastocytosis Include solitary mastocytoma, diffuse cuta neous mastocytosis (rare) and telangiectasia macuiariseruptiva perstans.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl attends clinic with her parents. She has short and uneven blonde hair with areas of "hair thinning". Her mother is concerned as she has not had a haircut for over 2 years and her hair seem to fall off easily. There is no family history of any hair abnormalities. Hair pull test was positive with multiple hairs pulled off easily. Microscopic examination of the hair showed absence of inner or outer root sheath and distorted hair bulbs. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
The differential diagnosis includes short anagen syndrome but the hair pull test would be negative.
Pili torti isa malformation of the hair shaft which is twisted about its axis. The hair is brittle and short and may be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
- Monilethrix is an autosomal dominant hair disorder in which the hair shaft is beaded and fragile.

questions.stem: You were asked to see a 3-week old baby born through forceps delivery. The paediatrician is concerned about a firm area on his upper back. Examination showed a mobile, firm, subcutaneous plaque. A biopsy taken by a paediatric dermatologist showed areas of necrosis in the adipocytes. The most important biochemical marker that needs regular monitoring is:
questions.explanation:
-The diagnosis is subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, often occurring following traumatic delivery.
Hypercalcaemia can occur and serum calcium levels need to be monitored.
Signs of hypercalcaemia in a baby include poor feeding, irritability and vomiting.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy from Tunisia presented with a palmo-plantar keratoderma and recurrent episodes of impetigo. He had uffered severe periodontitis at the age of 3 and as a consequence has lost most of his teeth. His nails were unaffected. His sister and mother had similar presentations. Both his parents are first cousins. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Papillon-Lefevre syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder that presents with palmo-plantar keraoderma, periodontitis and recurrent skin infections. In some cases hearing loss may occur.
In pachonychia congenital (PC) the nails are always abnormal (thickened and curved)
in addition to the presence of palmo-plantar keratoderma.
Two types of this autosomal dominant condition exist: PC-1 and PC-2.
In PC-1 (also called "Jadassohn-Lewandowsky type"), leukoplakia and follicular keratosis occur in addition to the PPK and nail abnormality.
In PC-2 (also called "Jackson-Lawler type"), the affected patients have natal teeth and cutaneous cysts (no leukoplakia and/or follicular keratosis).
Huriez syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant disorder in which palmo-plantar keratoderma is associated with sclerodactly and a high incidence of squamous cell carcinomas.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man if diagnosed with Fabry's disease by the metabolic medicine consultant. Which of the following type of angiokeratomas is associated with Fabry's disease?
questions.explanation:
These are the 5 types of angiokeratomas.
Angiokeratomas corporis diffusum is associated with Fabry's disease and often pre sents with multiple tiny angiokeratomas on the trunk and thighs.
Angiokeratomas of Mibelli occur on the dorsal aspects of the fingers and toes; whereas angiokeratomas of Fordyce occurs on the vulva or scrotum.
Angiokeratoma circumscriptum presents at birth or early in life (predominantly on the legs) as a large unilateral hyperkeratotic plaque with confluent keratotic papules.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl suffers from joint hypermobiiity, easy bruising and the tendency to develop atrophic scarring. Her father suffered from the same condition and died at the age of 46. Genetic testing showed a mutation on the gene COLPQAl. Which of the following investigations is highly recommended in this child?
questions.explanation:
-rhe history and findings here are suggestive of Ehlers-Danlos (EDS) type IV which is an autosomal dominant condition.
This is a vascular type of EDS with the risk of aortic dissection/rupture.
Echocardiography is essential in those patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following genodermatoses is not inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion?
questions.explanation:
Dyskeratosis congentia is an X-linked recessive disorder.
incontinentia pigmenti, Goltz syndrome, Conradi-Hunermann syndrome, Bazex syndrome, CHILD and MIDAS are some of the other X-linked dominant dermatological syndromes.

questions.stem: You are asked to see a premature neonate as he is born encased in shiny yellow covering. What is the most likely underlying dermatological condition?
questions.explanation:
Collodion babies are usually premature and are born encased in skin resembling a yellow, tight and shiny film.
Desquamation is usually complete by 2 to 3 weeks by which time the underlying skin disorder reveals itself.
The most common underlying diseases are lamellar ichthyosis and non-bullous congenital erythroderma.
Rarer conditions include Sjogren-Larsen syndrome, Dorfman-Chanarin syndrome (Neutral lipid storage disease), Gaucher's disease type-2, Trichothyodystrophy, Netherton syndrome, Hay-Well syndrome and Eciiodermal dysplasias.

questions.stem: A 7-month old boy presents with an itchy red rash on the skin that has been diagnosed as atopic dermatitis. He also has a distinctive circular scaling on the trunk. He was born with widespread red scaly skin. Examination of the scalp hair shows it to be short, spiky, lustreless and brittle. What is the hair abnormality in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features described above are those of Netherton syndrome.
Patients are erythrodermic at birth and later develop ichthyosis-ichthyosis lineariscircumflexa -circular scaling on the skin and a changing margin.
Trichorrhexlslnvaginata or Bamboo hair -refers to ball-and-socket-type hair-shaft deformity, which results in sparse, short, spiky, lustreless and brittle hair.
Allergic manifestations are commonly present.
These Include food allergies, hay fever, asthma, atopic eczema, angioedema and urticaria.

questions.stem: A 12-month old girl presents with subungual hyperkeratosis lifting the right little finger nail from the nail bed. She was born with a vesicular rash on her right forearm and hand. Which of the following stages in the condition is most likely to follow next?
questions.explanation:
incontinentia pigmenti is an X-linked dominant neurocutaneous syndrome.
Cutaneous features are seen in the following stages:
Stage 1 (vesicular) - present at birth or develop within the first 2 weeks of life in the vast majority. Red papules and vesicles on an erythematous base along Blaschko's lines and seen prP.dominantly on the extremities.
Stage 2 (verrucous) - develop in the first few weeks to months of life and resolve over weeks to months. Thickened, warty-appearing linear and whorled plaques on an erythematous base along Blaschko's lines.
Stage 3 (hyperpigmented)- streaks and whorls of brown or slate-gray pigmentation along Blaschko's lines. The location of the hyperpigmented lesions do not correlate with areas of prior skin involvement.
Stage 4 (atrophic/hypopigmented) - develop during adolescence and persist into adulthood. Hypopigmented, atrophic, and reticulate or linear patches can be observed on the lower extremities.
Besides cutaneous lesions, patients may have neurologic, ophthalmologic, and dental manifestations.
Mutations in the NEMO/IKK -gamma gene, on chromosome Xq28 are responsible for incontinentia pigmenti.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl presents with multiple skin-colored nodules. In addition she has numerous coffee-coloured patches and macules on her skin. Her mother has similar coffee-coloured patches and macules. You diagnose the condition as neurofibromatosis type-1 (NF-1). Her mother is concerned about the risk of malignancy. Which of the following is the commonest malignancy in NF-1?
questions.explanation:
The most common malignancy in NF-1 is neurofibrosarcoma.
Other malignancies include phaeochromocytoma, leukaemia, Wilm's tumour and rhabdomyosarcoma.

questions.stem: A 2.0-year-old man presents with facial angiofibromas and flesh-coloured plaques on the back. He is under the care of the neurologists for epilepsy. What is the earliest skin sign of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Tuberous sclerosis is a neurocutaneous disorder with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
The earliest skin sign in tuberous sclerosis is hypomelanotic macules.
Facial angiofibromas appear at the age of 4-9 years.
Peri-ungual and subungual fibromas develop at or after puberty.
Shagreen patch refers to an irregularly thickened, slightly elevated, flesh-coloured plaque, most commonly over the lumbosacral area. It develops in late childhood or adolescence.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man presents with facial angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules and flesh-coloured plaques on the back. He is under the care of the neurologists for epilepsy. The hypomelanotic macules appear polygonal or ash leaf in shape under Wood's light examination. What is the histological defect accounting for the hypomelanotic macules in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Abnormal melanin synthesis and impaired melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes accounts for the hypomelanotic macules seen in tuberous sclerosis.
These macules are best seen with Wood's light examination and appear polygonal or ash leaf shaped.

questions.stem: One of the following is not an inherited form of epidermolysis bullosa?
questions.explanation:
Inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is subclassified according to the level of skin separation seen in skin blisters on transmission electron microscopic analysis.
EB Simplex - intra-epidermal blistering associated with keratin gene mutations.
Hemidesmosomal EB - blistering skin disease with a level of separation that is inter-mediate between EB simplex and junctional EB.
Junctional EB - blister formation within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone due to defects of anchoring filaments.
Dystrophic EB - defects of the anchoring fibril, which results in s ublamina densa separation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is characterized by the development of peri-orificial granulation tissue?
questions.explanation:
Lethal junctional epidermolysis bullosa or Herlitz junctional epidermolysis bullosa patients is a life threatening disease.
Death rates of up to 40 % are seen in the first year of life and most of the surviving patients succumb before the age of 5 years.
Lethal junctional epidermolysis bullosa is characterized by generalized extensive blistering at birth.
Patients develop peri-orificial granulation tissue in infancy.

questions.stem: Which of the following syndromes has desmoid syndrome as an associated feature?
questions.explanation:
Desmoid tumours are deep-seated, aggressive, low-grade clonal benign musculoaponeurotic fibromatoses.
They have an infiltrative growth pattern and locally recur, but do not metastasize.
They have a mutation in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene (Sq21) and are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) syndrome and Gardner's syndrome.
They are classified as extra-abdominal or intra-abdominal.
Intra-abdominal desmoids have been associated in 10 to 15 % of patients with FAP and Gardner's syndrome, with the latter usually presenting as retroperitoneal tumors.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has been troubled with intense burning erythema with swelling on sun exposed sites within minutes of exposure to sunlight. This has been impacting negatively on his quality of life and he is therefore working and spending most of his time indoors. On further questioning, the erythema and swelling normally subsides within few hours. He has tried various sun avoidance measures and the use of high factor sun creams and is enquiring about systemic treatment. Which of the following systemic treatments is the first line treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Although immunosuppressive therapies can certainly be used with some degree of success in patients with solar urticaria, antihistamines remain first choice treatment.
UVB desensitisation can also be used in this condition provided that patients do not show sensitivity to that particular wavelength.
Erythema and wheals in solar urticaria develop within seconds to minutes following exposure to sunlight and almost always subside within 24 hours.

questions.stem: A 3-month old baby of consanguineous parents suffered severe sunburn following a limited exposure to sunlight. Examination showed dry skin but otherwise no abnormalities.There is no family history of photosensitivity. Which condition should be suspP.cted and looked for?
questions.explanation:
Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by marked photosensitivity, dry skin (hence the name xeroderma), abnormal freckling (hence pigmentosum) and a markedly increased risk of cutaneous neoplasms.
A less severe form exist called "variant" form of XP.
In XP marked sensitivity is to the UVB range is present hence the easy sunburns.
XP should always be considered in any baby who suffers easy sunburns and/or the presence of freckling under the age of 2 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not trigger or worsen porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)?
questions.explanation:
Serial phlebotomy is a treatment for PCT which can give clinicc::Iand biochemical remission and is particularly helpfu: in PCT patients with iron overload or haemochromatosis.
Low dose hydroxychloroquine (e.g. 200 mgtwice weekly) can be used particulcJrly in patients with normal or low iron levels.
Other triggers for PCT include hepatitis 8/C, genetic mutation for the uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase enzyme (the familial form), and rarely hepatocellular carcinoma.
Although PCT is the commonest cutaneous porphyria, variegate porphyria should always be excluded as this can be associated with fatal acute attacks and may present with cutaneous features similar to PCT.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with blisters on the back of her hands. Her rash is photosensitive and you suspect that she may have porphyria and carry out a porphyrin screen which is normal. You take a detailed drug history. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her rash?
questions.explanation:
The clinical picture is that of pseudoporphyria-porphyria cutanea tarda-like photosensitive blistering and skin fargility.
No hypertrichosis, hyperpigmentation or sclerodermoid changes are seen.
Causes of pseudoporphyria include- NSAID's, tetracyclines, haemodialysis, tanning booths, thlazides and frusemide.

questions.stem: Which of the following photosensitive or photo-aggravated conditions does not present with "blistering" following UV or visible light exposure?
questions.explanation:
Erythema multiforme can be aggravated following ultraviolet exposure (in particular if it was due to herpes simplex virus) and the photo-aggravated variant can be bullous In morphology.
Other conditions resulting In blistering following UV exposure include pseudoporphyria and bullous lupus erythematosus.
Actinic prurigo presents with excoriated papules or nodules (sometimes with plaques or an eczematous appearance) but not with blistering.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with pruritic papules on the face and dorsal hands following exposure to the sunlight. The symptoms require a minimum of 20 minutes exposure and appe,3r few hours afterwards. On examination there were excoriated papules on the nose, ears and cheeks with an excoriated lesion on the lower lip. Further history reveals conjunctival symptoms. There is no family history of photosensi tive disorders. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The history and findings of excoriated papules on the face with involvement of tne nose and cheilitis is typical of actinic prurigo.
Conjunctival involvement is common In this condition.
Unlike PLE, this condition tends to worsen as summer progresses and patients do not develop tolerance.
Hydroa vacciniforme presents with vesicles which become haemorrr,agic leaving pock-like scars.
Chronic actinic dermatitis is not seen in childhood and affects mostly middle-agea and old men.
Papules are the commonest morphological presentation of PLE (others ir,c.lude vesicles, urticarial, and eczematous variants) but are usually not excoriated and do not involve the lips and are not associ,fied with conjunctival symptoms.

questions.stem: In which of the following photosensitive disorders is sensitivity to the visible wavelength always present?
questions.explanation:
All porphyrias are sensitive to the visible wavelength of the radiation, hence sunblocks that only block UVB and to a lesser degree UVA are largely ineffective in this condition.
Solar urticaria is sensitive to predominantly UVA but the range of sensitivity can ex tend to involve both the UVB and visible light spectra.
Around half of the patients with chronic actinic dermatitis exhibit photosensitivity in the visible wavelength.

questions.stem: In which of the following photosensitive disorders is monochromator reading nearly always abnormal?
questions.explanation: Although any photosensitive disorder can have abnormal monochromator readings, these are nearly always(technique dependent) abnormal in chronic actinic dermatitis, solar urticaria, porphyria, and to a lesser degree drug-induced photosensitivity.

questions.stem: Which of the following - predominantly childhood - photosensitive disorders is not inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern?
questions.explanation:
Although actinic prurigo has a strong association with HLA-DRBl*0407, the condition is not inherited through the Mendelian pattern.
Rothmund Thomson syndrome is associated with photosensitivity, poikiloderma, short stature, skeletal dysplasia and juvenile cataracts.
The condition can predispose to squamous cell carcinomas and osteosarcomas.
Bloom's syndrome is characterized by photosensitivity and poikiloderma but growth retardation is more marked and the risk of developing malignancies is much greater but these tend to be leukaemias early in life and solid organ tumours later.

questions.stem: Which of the following surfaces reflect ultraviolet rays the most?
questions.explanation:
Snow can reflect around 90% of the UV rays followed by water and sand.
Sun protection advice should always include the risk of reflection from those surfaces.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding photodynamic therapy is false?
options: Photodynamic therapy is associated with a better cosmetic outcome than cyrotherapy in the treatment of superficial basal cell carcinoma (sBCC).
Photodynamic therapy is recommended for the treatment of small squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs).
Surgical excision is more effective than photodynamic therapy for treatment of nodular basal cell carcinoma (nBCCs).
Topical methylarninolevulinate and 5-arninolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy are effective treatments for sBCCs.
Topical methylaminolevulinate and 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy are equally effective in the treatment of small nBCCs.
questions.explanation:
Topical methyl aminolevulinate and 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy are effecitive treatments for sBCCs.
Results of a study directly comparing these two photosensitisers in treatment of nBCCs showed no difference in efficacy.
Surgical excision is more effective than fractionated illuminated 5-aminolevulinic acid photodynamlc therapy for treatment of nBCCs.
For patients with sBCCs, methyl-aminolevulinate photodynamic therapy has a similar response to that of cryosurgery but cosmetic outcome is better with photodynamic therapy.
Since data are scarce for the efficacy of topical photodynamic therapy in primary cutaneous invasive SCCs, topical therapy cannot be recommended for sec.

questions.stem: Which of the following photosensitive disorders is typically inherited in a non-autosomal recessive pattern?
questions.explanation:
Porphyrias with cutaneous involvement are, without exception, photosensitive and can be classified depending on hepatic and/or e;ythropoietic involvement.
Hepatic porphyrias with cutaneous involvement present with i.?ss acute skin changes and concern:
Porphyria cutanea tarda: Inheritance: Autosomal dominant (20-30%) or acquired. Enzyme defect: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase
Hereditary coproporphyria: Inheritance: Autosomal dominant. Enzyme defect:
Coproporphyrinogen oxidase
Mixed hepatic c:1nd erythropoietic porphyria withcutaneous involvement also demonstrates less acute skin change and concerns:
Variegate Porphyria. Inheritance: Autosomal dominant. Enzyme defect: Pro toporphyrinogen oxidase
Erythropoietic porphyrias manifests with acute skin change and concern:
Erythropoietic protoporphyria: Inheritance: Mostly autosomal dominant (but autosomal recessive cases have been reported)
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria: Inheritance: Autosomal recessive. Enzyme defect: Ferrochelatase
X-linked sideroblastic anaemia: Inheritance: X-linked recessive defect in the ALAS2 gene. Enzyme defect: Erythroid ALA-synthase Other autosomal recessive photosensitive disorders to be aware of include:
Rothmund-Thompson syndrome
Smith-Lemi-Opitz syndrome
Trichothiodystrophy Xeroderma pigmentosum

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman develops a vesicular eruption over her lower lip after starting PUVA for vitiligo. What is the most likely cause?
options: Photosensitivity due to an associated autoimmune connective tissue disorder.
Fixed drug eruption to ingested psoralen.
questions.explanation:
Narrow-band UVB cian also elicit HSV reactivation
Other side effects shared by both treatment modalities include photo-aging and increased risk of skin cancer (although the risk with narrow-band UVB is considerably lower).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with skin phenotype 2 is to start narrow-band UVB for poorly controlled, chronic plaque psoriasis. What is the maximum number of sessions he can have in a lifetime?
questions.explanation:
The maximum number of sessions for narrow-band UVB is 300.
A 48-hour gap is needed between each session, allowing 3 sessions per week.
For PUVA a maximum of 250 sessions are allowed over a lifetime.
A 72-hour gap is needed between each session, allowing 2 sessions per week.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy presented with his mother with a history of extreme photosensitivity with a burning and painful sensation within minutes following sun exposure. He had on several occasions, been noted to have swelling of the hands following sun exposure. Hiselder brother has similar symptoms and is currently takingbeta-carotene tablets. The enzyme defect In this condition is:
questions.explanation:
Ferrochelatase isthe enzyme defect in erythropoietic protoporphyria which typically presents with pain and burning sensation, extreme sun sensitivity within minutes to exposure of sunlight and may be associated with swelling of the hands.
Protoporphyrinogen oxidase is the enzyme defect in variegate porphyria.
Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase is the enzyme defect in porphyrio cutanea tarda.
In hereditary coproporphyria the defect is in coproporphyrinogenoxidase.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has two patches of Bowen's disease on the left lower leg, previously treated with cryotherapy with little success. A consultant dermatologist suggested treatment with photodynamic therapy and the use of methyl levulenic acid (MAL). What should be the approximate application time of the MAL for treatment with alight source?
questions.explanation:
The ideal application time for MAL is 3 hours, to ensure maximum affectivity.
Shorter duration of application may result in ineffective therapy.

questions.stem: Which of the following wavelengths is responsible for immediate tanning?
questions.explanation:
Immediate tanning occurs within 5 to 10 minutes of exposure to UVA irradiation (often referred to as immediate pigment darkening "IPD").
It represents melanosomal relocation from the perikaryon to melanocytic dendrites.
It fades within minutes to days.
It does not provide photoprotection and does not increase epidermal melanin level.
It is predominantly visible in darker individuals.

questions.stem: Photosensitivity is not a presenting feature of one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Acute intermittent porphyria results from defects in porphobilinogen-deaminase.
Attacks are characterised by abdominal pain, psychiatric symptoms and peripheral neuropathy.
There are no skin manifestations in acute intermittent porphyria.
Variegate porphyria presents similarly to PCT but with the presence of acute symptoms; therefore it is essential to exclude this diagnosis in patients suspected of PCT through urine porphyrin measurements together with a plasma porphyrin scan.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl was referred to the dermatologist with a history of sun-sensitivity resulting in small papules and vesicles, often on the face and predominantly the nose. Some of the vesicles became haemorrhagic and had healed with crusting. Examination revealed some atrophic scars on the face and the arms where the haemorrhagic vesicles were present. Provocation tests later revealed a few papules and vesicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Hydroa vacciniforme isa photosensitive disorder which is often diagnosed in children and tends to improve later in adult life.
Typically, the lesions present with papules and vesicles, some of which may become haemorrhagic and heal with crusting and erosions. Atrophic scars can be seen as a result.
Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive photosensitive disorder which often presents with severe photosensitivity, dryness of the skin and abnormal freckling.
Patients with XP are at a greater risk of developing skin tumours at very early age.
.., Polymorphic light eruption is a non-scarring idiopathic photosensitive disorder.

questions.stem: In which of the following is the risk of developing squamous cell carcinomas the highest?
questions.explanation:
Multiple factors contribute to the development of squamous cell carcinomas, such as immunosuppression, ultraviolet therapy, chronic wounds, arsenic ingestion, pre-existent dysplastic lesions and previous radiotherapy.
The risk of developing skin cancers following treatment with PUVA is higher than that compared to UVB and this risk is particularly high when PUVA is administered in a patient who was previously treated with ciclosporin.

questions.stem: Which of the following photodermatoses is not seen in children?
questions.explanation:
Chronic actinic dermatitis is mostly seen in elderly men, although women and young adults may also be affected.
It is not seen in children and the condition is often persistent.
Multiple contact allergies are often associated with thecondition.

questions.stem: Which of the following photosensitive disorders is least likely to give symptoms shortly following exposure to UV or visible light?
questions.explanation:
Lupus erythematosus, actinic prurigo and hydroa vacciniforme do not generally give immediate symptoms following exposure to light.
Polymorphic light eruption (PLE) typically has a latency period of several hours but a less common variant exist in which short exposure to light triggers the rash (rapid onset PLE).
Drugs should always be included in the differential of immediate photosensitivity, particularly if the symptoms occur in a patient who previously could tolerate UV and visible light exposure.

questions.stem: At which level does lm NaCl cause a split in the skin?
questions.explanation: Lamina lucida is the weakest part of the basement membrane.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a key component of inner dense plaque?
questions.explanation:
Desmosomal proteins fall into three major gene families:
Plakins -desmoplakin.
Armadillo proteins-plakoglobin and plakophilins.
Desmosomal cadherins-desmogleins and desmocollins.
Plakins and armadillo proteins are found in the plaque.
Desmosomal cadherins are extracellular amino-termini of transmembrane proteins, which comprise the desmogleins.
Desmoplakin is the major inner plaque component.

questions.stem: Sebaceous glands are absent in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Palms and soles do not contain sebaceous glands or hair follicles.
Facial skin and in particular the nose contain the largest number of sebaceous glands.

questions.stem: Epidermal desmosomes serve to adhere the cells together due to the presence of various glycoproteins. Which of the following components of the desmosomes is not targeted in paraneoplastic pemphigus?
questions.explanation:
Corneodesmosin is targeted by the autosomal dominant rare condition hypotrichosis simplex of the scalp.
Plakoglobin is also targeted in the inherited disorder of Naxos disease.
Desmoglein-1 is targeted in pemphigus foliaceous, whereas desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein-1) are targeted in pemphigus vulgaris.
A rare variant of pemphigus called IgA-pemphigus results from antibodies targeting desmocollins.

questions.stem: Eccrine sweat glands are present in which one of the following sites?
questions.explanation:
External auditory canal, lips, clitoris and labia minora do not have eccrine glands.
Apart from the above, approximately 1.6 to 4.0 million eccrine sweat glands are distributed over the entire body skin surface.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is involved in the Lewis reaction (also known as the hunter's reflex)?
questions.explanation:
.., The Lewis reaction/ hunter's reflex describes the normal pallor of fingers and other extremities in response to cold.
The glomus apparatus or body is a dermal structure consisting of an arteriovenous shunt under autonomic nervous system control. Most numerous in the extremities it plays an important role in temperature regulation by shunting blood away from the skin surface when exposed to cold temperature.
The eccrine and pilosebaceous units also play a role in temperature regulation but via sweat production and hair contracture, respectively.
The Pacinian corpuscle detects vibration and the Meissner's corpuscle detects fine touch.

questions.stem: You wish to undertake a research study to assess circadian variation in keratinocyte RNA levels. Which of the following research techniques would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
A useful aid-memoire is SNoW DRoP, where southern blotting relates to DNA, Northern blotting to RNA and Western blotting to protein.
Eastern blotting allows analysis of post-translational protein modifications (PTM).
Reverse PCR would be used to amplify RNA.

questions.stem: What is the trans-epidermal cycle time in normal skin?
questions.explanation:
Starting in the basal layer it takes 14 days for the maturing keratinocyte to reach to stratum corneum and a further 14 days to reach to the very surface of thi,sayer, allow ing it to be shed.
The trans-epidermal time is considerably shorter in diseases such as psoriasis and is prolonged in the elderly.

questions.stem: A patient is carrying a CTLA-4 gene mutation. Which of the following diseases would you wish to exclude?
questions.explanation:
The CTLA-4 protein is found on the surface of cytotoxic r cells and functions to down-regulate immune responses.
Mutations in the gene encoding this protein predispose to autoimmune disease including coeliac disease, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid dis ease and lupus erythematosus.
Similarly, pharmacological inhibition of CTLA-4, with agents such as ipilimumab, can also trigger autoimmune phenomena.

questions.stem: Which type of collagen is the most abundant in the dermis?
questions.explanation:
The dermis is composed of type 1 collagen that forms nearly 80%, with nearly 15- 20% type 3 collagen and a small amount of type 5 collagen.
Collagens provide the tensile strength in the dermis, whereas the elastic fibres pro vide the elasticity of the dermis.
The origin of the collagen is from the fibroblasts which are found in the dermis.
There are 2.8 types of collagen.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a ubiquitous component of the basement membrane?
questions.explanation:
Basement membranes contain collagenous and non-collagenous glycoproteins and proteoglycans.
Collagen IV, laminin, nidogen, and heparan sulfate proteoglycanperlecan are ubiquitially present in all basement membrane.

questions.stem: Which of the following resultsfrom altered a6 4 integrin?
questions.explanation:
Keratin 5 and 14 mutations result in epidermolysis bullosa simplex.
Collagen XVII/BP180 - linear IgA disease.
Collagen VII - Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Laminin 332/laminin-5 - Junctional epldermolysis bullosa - Herlitz and non-Herlitz.
a6P4 integrin - Cicatritial pemphigoid.

questions.stem: Filaggrin mutations are not associated with one of the following disorders?
options: Allergic rhinitis in patients with atopic dermatitis.
Asthma in patients with atopic dermatitis.
questions.explanation:
Mutations in the filaggrin gene are associated with ichthyosisvulgaris.
Mutations in filaggrin are also a risk factor for atopic dermatitis and are associated with disease severity.
Among patients with atopic dermatitis, mutated filaggrin is associated with asthma, allergic rhinitis and allergic sensitisation.
Mutated filaggrin is not independently associated with asthma.
Mutated filaggrin predicts a more severe course in alopecia areata.

questions.stem: A 4-week old Afro-Caribbean boy presents to the dermatology clinic with pigmented macules on the trunk which followed clearance of pus-filled spots. The following statement is true:
options: The clinical course is protracted and may last many years.
The rash is more common in Afro-Caribbean babies.
questions.explanation:
The clinical picture described above is that of transient neonatal pustular melanosis.
It affects approximately 5% of black neonates and <1% of white neonates.
Transient vesiculopustules which resolve in 48 hours give way to pigmented macules.
The pigmented macules usually resolve within 3 months.
The pustule is subcorneal and neutrophilic.
Unlike erythema toxicumneonatorum, peripheral eosinophilia is absent.
The condition is self-limiting and no treatment is requiied.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a cause of exogenous ochronosis?
questions.explanation:
Exogenous ochronosis results from the use of certain medications, including hydroquinone, anti-malarialsand products containing resorcinol, phenol, mercury, and piaic acid.
It presents as asymptomatic hyperpigmentation of the face, sides and back of the neck, back, and extensor sites of the extremities.
Yellowish-brown globules accumulate in the papillary dermis.
Unlike endogenous ochronosis, there is no articular, renal, or cardiovacular involvement.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old Afro-Caribbean man reported a five year history of persistent painful purulent draining scalp lesions accompanied by p ogressively worsening alopecia. Physical examination reveals pustules, nodules and fluctuant abscesses, and multiple palpable cervical lymph nodes. Pus waseasily drained from some of the abscesses and there were communicating sinuses visible. For thiscondition, which of the following statementsis incorrect?
options: Anti-fungal treatment is not indicated in this condition.
Arthralgia may occur in some cases.
Basal cell carcinoma may complicate long-standing disease.
Staphylococcus is often the most commonly cultured pathogen from secondarily infected lesions.
The pathogenesis of thiscondition relates to primary follicular occlusion disorder.
questions.explanation:
Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp belongs together with hidradenitis suppurativa and acne conglobata to the primary follicular occlusion disorders.
Arthralgia can occur in some cases as a systemic manifestation of the disease.
Squamous cell carcinoma and not basal cell carcinoma may complicate long-standing disease.
Treatment is often disappointing; however there is no role for anti-fungal therapy.

questions.stem: The dermatology registrar in the department excised an atypical looking mole on the shoulder of a 24-year-old sun worshipper. Histology showed superficial spreading melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1.3 mm without ulceration. You are referring the patient to the plastic surgeon for re-excision. What should be the re-excision margins?
questions.explanation:
5 mm is the margin is employed for melanoma in-situ and lentigo maligna (melano ma in situ in sun-damaged skin).
The guidelines suggest that in thin melanomas (less than 1 mm in depth), these should be excised with a margin of at least 1 cm and for melanomas, between 1.01-2 mm a margin of 2 cm when pcs.sible.
2 mm margin is the initial margin used for atypical naevi as was the case here.

questions.stem: Which of the following tumours is most likely to develop in organ transplant recipients?
questions.explanation:
Although the incidence of cutaneous tumours and dysplastic lesions is greatly in creased in patients with organ transplantation due to immune suppression, the risk of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in particular is greatly increased (x 60-250) and the usual basal cell carcinoma: sec incidence ratio of 4:1is reversed.
The risk of basal cell carcinoma and melanoma is also increased but to a lesser de gree compared to secs.

questions.stem: Which of the following presents with 'buttonholing' or 'dimple sign' on lateral pressure?
questions.explanation:
Dermatofibromas are firm, indurated, but mobile common mesenchymal lesions.
Lateral compression of dermatofibroma produces a dimple-like depression in tht:
overlying skin ("buttonholing").

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding leukaemia cutis is incorrect?
options: Children with leukaemia are more likely to be affected than adults.
Cutaneous signs can appear prior to systemic involvement.
Mostly associated with acute myeloid leukaemias.
Portends a good prognosis for theileukaemia.
Presence of leukaemia cutis is often associated with extra-medullary haemopolesis.
questions.explanation:
Leukaemia cutis is often associated with a poor prognosis and may precede the detection of systemic disease when it is then referred to as "aleukaemia cutis".
Treatment is very challenging and is mainly palliative.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the commonest clinical subtype of basal cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Roughly 80% of all ba al-cell carcinomas occur on the head and neck.
In addition to the classic rodent ulcer with an indurated edge and ulcerated centre (nodular or cystic), superficial, morphoeic, and pigmented basal-cell carcinomas are other common subtypes.
10-40% of basal-cell carcinomas contain a mixed pattern of two or more of these histological subtypes, drawing attention to the need for a clinicopathological diagnosis.
By contrast with nodulocystic basal-cell carcinoma-which is the most common subtype, usually presenting on the head and neck-superficial basal-cell carcinomas predominantly present on the trunk.
5% of allbasal-cell carcinomas are morphoeic lesions, which have ill-defined borders, can be difficult to diagnose clinically, and often present late.

questions.stem: One of the following syndromes does not predispose to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
The following are syndromes predisposing to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma:
Xeroderma pigmentosum - autosomal recessive; multiple epidermal skin cancers in childhood; increased susceptibility to DNA damage; abnormal DNA base excision repair.
Albinism - part or complete failure to produce melanin in the skin and eyes.
Muir-Torre syndrome-autosomal dominant; germline mutations in genes involved in DNA mismatch repair; sebaceous neoplasms in association with internal malignancy.
KID (keratosis, icthyosis, deafness) syndrome - development of invasive squamous cell carcinoma within dysplastic lesions.
Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa - autosomal recessive m'?.chano-bullous disorder; mutations in the human type VII collagen gene (COL.7Al).
Fanconi anaemia - autosomal recessive; congenital malformations; bone-marrow failure; development of squamous-cell carcinoma and other cancers.
Rothmund-Thompson syndrome - autosomal recessive; progressive poikiloderma including alopecia, dystrophic teeth and nails, juvenile cataracts, short stature, hypogonadism, and bone defects.
Werner syndrome - early ageing; excess cancer risk; high incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus; early atherosclerosis; ocular cataracts; osteoporosis.
Others - Hereditary non-polyposis coli; dyskeratosis congenit-a; Huriez syndrome; LiFraumeni syndrome and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a poor prognostic factor in basal cell carcinomas?
questions.explanation: Factors determining poor prognosis in basal cell carcinomas include: morphceic lesions, tumour size) 5 cm (giant), deeper lesions, centrofacial and ears, infiltrative and micronodular histological subtypes, histological features of aggression including perineural or perivascular involvement, or both and recurrent lesions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for the development of Bowen's disease?
questions.explanation:
Gorlin's syndrome predisposes to multiple basal cell carcinomas and not Bowen's disease or squamous cell carcinoma.
Other features of Gorlin's syndrome include palmoplantar pits, odontogenic jaw cysts, frontal bossing, medulloblastomas, lipomas and hypogonadism.
HPV can cause Bowen's disease and is one of the aetiologic factors for the development of squamous cell carcinomas in transplant patients.

questions.stem: Which one of the following factors does not confer a higher risk of recurrence for basal cell carcinomas?
options: Tumour around the lips or ears.
Tumour with poorly defined clinical margins.
questions.explanation:
Recurrence risk for basal cell carcinomas depends on several factors iniluding size, site, clinical margins, histological subtype/features of aggressive tumour, and failure of previous treatments.
High-risk sites include areas around the eyes, nose, lips and ears.
The presence of a metaplastic, Infiltrative, morphoeic or micro-nodular histological subtype is regarded as a high risk tumour.

questions.stem: Regarding the use of radiotherapy in basal cell carcinoma (BCC), which statement is false?
options: Radiotherapy can be used as an adjuvant treatment.
Radiotherapy can be used in the treatment of primary BCC.
Suitable as a mode of treatment for radiorecurrent BCC.
Suitable as a mode of treatment for surgically recurrent BCC.
questions.explanation:
Radiorecurrent BCCs should not be retreated with radiotherapy and should be excised surgically.
Radiotherapy may be more preferable as first-line therapy in elderly or infirm pa tients in whom surgery may not be possible.

questions.stem: Which of the following benign lesions can arise from a congenital naevus sebaceous?
questions.explanation:
